lessons.unit: Unit 1: Natural hazards (AQA 3.1.1.1)
lessons.title: What is a natural hazard, and why does risk vary?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can the same hazard kill thousands in one place and almost nobody in another?
objectives: Define a natural hazard and classify hazards as tectonic, weather or other types
Explain why some hazards pose a greater risk to people than others
Explain how vulnerability, capacity to cope and the nature of the hazard affect risk
successCriteria: All: define hazard and give two examples of each main type
Most: explain at least two factors that increase risk
Some: use hazard, vulnerability and capacity to cope together to explain a contrast between two places
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: using a simple risk ratio to compare places
lessons.smsc: Moral: our duty of care (amanah) to protect vulnerable people; reflecting on the power of creation with humility

keywords.def: a natural event that threatens people or property
the probability that people will be harmed by a hazard
how likely people are to be harmed because of where and how they live
the ability of people to prepare for, survive and recover from a hazard
the size or strength of a hazard event

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two weather events that can be dangerous in the UK.
What is the difference between weather and climate?
Give one way that rainfall can become dangerous to people.

teach.heading: Types of natural hazard

head: Type
Examples
Main cause
rows: Slope, rock, weather and vegetation together

teach.note: Start by asking for examples before showing the table. Make the point that tectonic hazards come from inside the Earth and weather hazards from the atmosphere, but they can combine: an earthquake can trigger a tsunami or landslide; a storm can trigger a flood. AQA questions on 3.1.1.1 expect you to define a hazard and to state types, so insist on the exact definition: an event that threatens people or property. Stress that without people there is no hazard, only a natural event.

teach.heading: Hazard or disaster?

misconception.wrong: A natural hazard is the same thing as a natural disaster.
misconception.right: A hazard is the threat. It becomes a disaster when it meets vulnerable people and causes serious losses.

teach.note: Use two imagined villages: the same flood hits both, one has a warning system and raised homes. Which suffers a disaster? Pupils should see that disaster depends on people, not only the event. This is a common one-mark loss in definition questions. Link to amanah: we are asked to care for people and places, and reducing vulnerability is part of that care.

teach.heading: Factors that affect risk

left.title: The hazard itself
points: Magnitude: how strong
Frequency: how often
Duration: how long it lasts
Predictability: can we warn people?

right.title: People and place
points: Vulnerability: poverty, poor housing
Capacity to cope: money, planning, services
Population density and urban growth
Living in risky areas such as flood plains

teach.note: Ask pupils to place each factor in the correct column on mini-whiteboards. Explain that hazards that strike suddenly with no warning (earthquakes) tend to be riskier than slow ones (drought), even at similar magnitude, because people cannot act in time. Stress that capacity to cope is mainly about money, governance and preparation. A simplified model is: risk rises with the size of the hazard and with vulnerability, and falls with capacity to cope. Present this as a teaching model, not a precise formula.

teach.heading: Model answer: explain why risk differs

model.problem: Two cities are each struck by a magnitude 7 earthquake. City A is in a low-income country with crowded, poorly built homes. City B is in a high-income country with strict building codes. Explain why risk is greater in City A. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1: homes in City A are poorly built, so they collapse and more people are trapped (vulnerability).
Point 2: City A has less money for emergency services, hospitals and rescue equipment (low capacity to cope).
Point 3: high population density means more people are close to the hazard.
Link each point to risk with a connective: 'which means', 'therefore', 'as a result'.
model.answer: Risk is greater in City A because its buildings are poorly built, so they are more likely to collapse and kill people, which makes people more vulnerable. City A also has less money for rescue teams and hospitals, so it has a lower capacity to cope and more people die as a result.

teach.note: I do. Show how each mark is a developed point: a fact then a reason. Underline the connectives in the model. Pupils often list factors without explaining how they change risk. The two cities are imagined: the case studies in the next lessons give real figures.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which change would most reduce the risk to a coastal community from storms?
options: A new early-warning system and storm shelters
More people building homes on the shore
check.why: B reduces vulnerability and increases capacity to cope. A, C and D each increase risk. Pupils choosing C may think the question is about location only.

teach.note: Answer: B. Ask a pupil who chose C to explain; use it to revisit that vulnerability grows when more people live in danger zones.

practice: Classify each hazard as tectonic, weather or flooding: volcanic eruption, drought, blizzard, tsunami, river flood, heatwave.
Complete the sentence stems: 'Vulnerability means...' and 'Capacity to cope means...'.
independent: Core: Define the term 'natural hazard'. (2 marks) Give two factors that can increase the risk from a hazard. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain why some hazards pose a greater risk to people than others. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'Poverty is the most important factor affecting the risk from natural hazards.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Which of these is a hazard and which is a disaster: a river rising, or a river flooding 500 homes with deaths?
Return to the big question: give two reasons the same hazard can have different effects in two places.
lessons.homework: Find a news report of a hazard in the last five years. Make a table with the hazard, the place, and two factors that increased or reduced the risk. About 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND: sort-card activity for hazards types and a sentence frame for 'X means risk is higher because...'. EAL: picture glossary for hazard, risk, vulnerable. Stretch: compare how risk might change over time in one place as it urbanises.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Tectonic hazards (AQA 3.1.1.2)
lessons.title: Plate tectonics: Earth's structure, distribution and plate margins
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do earthquakes and volcanoes happen in some places and not others?
objectives: Describe the structure of the Earth and how convection currents move plates
Describe the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes
Explain what happens at constructive, destructive and conservative margins
successCriteria: All: label the layers of the Earth and name three plate margin types
Most: describe the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes using named plates or places
Some: explain in sequence how a destructive margin produces both earthquakes and volcanoes
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: convection and density
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the scale and order of the Earth as part of creation

keywords.def: the thin, solid outer layer of the Earth
the thick layer of hot rock beneath the crust that flows very slowly
the boundary where two tectonic plates meet
when a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate
the point on the surface directly above the focus of an earthquake
the point underground where an earthquake starts

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two types of hazard from last lesson and say which are tectonic.
Define vulnerability.
Why might a poorer country be more at risk from the same earthquake as a richer country?

teach.heading: Structure of the Earth

head: Layer
Approximate size
State
rows: Very hot rock; solid but flows slowly

teach.note: Sketch the layers on the board. Emphasise that the plates are the crust plus the rigid top of the mantle, and they float on the flowing mantle beneath. Oceanic crust is thinner and denser than continental crust; this matters for subduction. Sizes are approximate; pupils need the pattern, not the exact numbers. Misconception: the mantle is liquid. It is solid rock that flows very slowly over millions of years.

teach.heading: Why do plates move?
bullets: Heat from the core drives convection currents in the mantle.
Hot mantle rises, spreads, cools and sinks.
Plates are dragged or pushed: slab pull and ridge push.
Plates move only a few centimetres each year.
teach.note: Compare to a pan of thick soup heating slowly. Ask: why do the plates move so slowly we cannot feel it? Plates move roughly as fast as fingernails grow, around 2 to 10 cm per year depending on the plate. Slab pull: the cold, dense sinking edge pulls the rest of the plate. Ridge push: new crust at ridges slides downhill. AQA only requires the convection explanation at GCSE, so do not overload.

teach.heading: Plate margins

head: Margin
Movement
Example
Hazards and landforms
rows: Shield volcanoes, fissures, weak shallow earthquakes
Composite volcanoes, powerful earthquakes, ocean trench
Plates slide past at different speeds
Fold mountains, earthquakes, little volcanic activity

teach.note: Use a physical model such as two books or hands. The collision margin is not always listed separately, but it is needed for Nepal in the case-study lesson. Common error: saying earthquakes occur only at destructive margins. They occur at all of them. Volcanoes occur only where magma can reach the surface: constructive and destructive margins. Link Iceland to the constructive margin: it sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

teach.heading: Destructive margin: how it works
cycle: Dense oceanic plate is pushed beneath continental plate
Plates stick; friction and pressure build
Sudden release: earthquake
Sinking plate melts; magma rises
Eruption forms a composite volcano
teach.note: Walk through the sequence slowly. Make pupils say 'which causes' between steps. Point out two outcomes from one process: earthquakes (stuck plates snapping free) and volcanoes (melting plate). Ask: why is this cycle repeated? Because the plates keep moving, so pressure builds again. The Andes, the Pacific Ring of Fire and Japan are linked to this process.

teach.heading: Skill: describe a distribution

model.problem: Describe the global distribution of volcanoes. (3 marks)
steps: Name the pattern: many follow lines along plate margins.
Name an area with a cluster: the Pacific Ring of Fire around the edge of the Pacific Ocean.
Name an area with a line and a gap: along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge but few in the centre of continents.
Use compass directions or ocean names, not just 'everywhere'.
model.answer: Volcanoes are mostly found along plate margins. There is a large cluster around the edge of the Pacific Ocean, called the Ring of Fire, and a line in the Atlantic along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Few are found in the middle of continents.

teach.note: I do. Describe means say what you see, not why. Pupils lose marks by explaining instead of describing. Have a map on screen if possible. Real exceptions exist: hotspot volcanoes such as Hawaii are not at margins, but this goes beyond the spec so mention only for stretch.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which plate margin can produce earthquakes but not volcanoes?
check.why: At a conservative margin plates slide past, so no magma rises. Distractor B is tempting because destructive margins produce both.

teach.note: Answer: C. Ask pupils who chose B to name where a volcano forms at a destructive margin (above the melting sinking plate).

practice: Label a diagram of the Earth: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.
Draw and label a diagram of a destructive margin with the trench, volcano and earthquake zone.
independent: Core: Describe the structure of the Earth. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how earthquakes and volcanoes are formed at a destructive plate margin. (4 marks)
Stretch: Compare the hazards found at a constructive margin with those at a conservative margin. (4 marks)
exit: Which margin type would you find in Iceland?
Return to the big question: give one reason volcanoes occur near plate margins.
lessons.homework: Draw an annotated map of the Pacific Ring of Fire with at least five named places (for example Japan, Chile, California).
lessons.send: SEND: pre-labelled margin diagrams and a card sort of 'what happens next'. EAL: key terms with images, say each aloud. Stretch: explain why hotspot volcanoes like Hawaii do not fit the margin pattern.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Tectonic hazards (AQA 3.1.1.2)
lessons.title: Tectonic hazards: effects, responses, and reducing the risk
lessons.bigQuestion: If tectonic hazards are so dangerous, why do millions of people live with them?
objectives: Distinguish primary from secondary effects and immediate from long-term responses
Explain why people continue to live in tectonically active areas
Evaluate monitoring, prediction, protection and planning as ways to reduce risk
successCriteria: All: sort effects into primary and secondary and responses into immediate and long-term
Most: give three reasons people live near tectonic hazards
Some: judge which risk-reduction strategy is most effective, with reasons
lessons.crossCurricular: Technology: seismometers and building engineering
lessons.smsc: Moral: compassion and help for those affected; fairness in sharing resources between rich and poor countries

keywords.def: damage caused directly by the hazard itself
damage that follows later because of the primary effects
action in the hours and days after a hazard
action in the months and years that follow
forecasting when and where a hazard will happen
measuring changes that might warn of a hazard

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the three main types of plate margin.
State what happens at a conservative margin.
Explain what 'subduction' means.

teach.heading: Effects and responses

head: Timing
Effects
Responses
rows: Buildings collapse; people killed or injured; roads and power cut
Search and rescue; first aid; emergency shelters; food, water and medicine
Fires, landslides, tsunami; disease; unemployment; homelessness
Rebuilding; new building codes; money from insurance or aid; restoring jobs

teach.note: Be exact with the terms. Primary effects happen as a direct result of the ground shaking or the eruption. Secondary effects are knock-on, for example fires from broken gas pipes or disease from damaged water supplies. Immediate responses are in the first hours and days; long-term responses take months or years. The table headers deliberately pair the two vocabularies so pupils can see both. Ask for examples of each from their own knowledge. Case-study detail follows next lesson.

teach.heading: Why do people stay?
bullets: Fertile volcanic soils support farming.
Geothermal energy, minerals and tourism provide jobs.
Family ties, culture and no money to move.
Hazard is rare, or people believe it will not happen to them.
teach.note: Ask: would you leave your home? Pupils usually say yes, then realise how much money, family and work are tied to a place. In Iceland, geothermal power heats most homes. Around Mount Vesuvius and Mount Etna, soils are fertile. Many people are not aware of the danger or have no choice. Be sensitive: some pupils may have family in earthquake zones; keep the tone respectful and factual.

teach.heading: Four ways to reduce risk

left.title: Before: monitor and predict
points: Seismometers record small tremors
Gas and ground tilt measured on volcanoes
Volcano warnings sometimes possible
Earthquakes cannot be reliably predicted

right.title: Before: protect and plan
points: Earthquake-proof buildings: cross-bracing, shock absorbers, deep foundations
Drills and emergency kits
Land-use zoning away from risk areas
Evacuation routes and shelters

teach.note: Explain that monitoring uses instruments, prediction is the forecast, protection is the physical design, and planning is the organisation (evacuation routes, zoning, drills). Ask: why can volcanoes sometimes be predicted but earthquakes not? Volcanoes give measurable warning signs such as rising gas and small tremors; the build-up to earthquakes is not reliably measurable. Wealthy places can afford more of all four, which links back to capacity to cope.

teach.heading: Skill: evaluate a strategy

model.problem: 'Earthquake-proof building is the best way to reduce the risk from earthquakes.' How far do you agree? (4 marks)
steps: Start with an argument for: it protects lives when shaking starts and works with no warning.
Add a limit: it is expensive, so poorer countries cannot build all homes this way.
Compare to another strategy: planning such as drills and evacuation costs less but does not stop collapse.
Make a judgement: it is the most effective, but best combined with planning in poorer places.
model.answer: I partly agree. Earthquake-proof building is very effective because it saves lives even without warning. However it is expensive, so poorer countries cannot afford it for all homes. Cheaper methods such as practice drills are less effective alone, so the best approach combines building design with planning.

teach.note: I do. Evaluation questions need an argument for, an argument against, and a clear judgement. Many pupils stop after a for-and-against list. Teach the judgement stem: 'Overall, ... because ...'. Reuse in the 6- and 9-mark questions in the exam.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is a secondary effect of an earthquake?
options: Fire caused by broken gas pipes
A new building code being written
check.why: B follows from the primary shaking. A is primary. C is an immediate response and D is a long-term response.

teach.note: Answer: B. Pupils who chose C or D have mixed effects with responses; revisit the table.

practice: Sort these into primary / secondary effect or immediate / long-term response: landslide, search and rescue, rebuilding schools, people killed by collapsing buildings, cholera outbreak.
Give three reasons why people live near volcanoes.
independent: Core: State two ways of monitoring a volcano. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain why earthquakes are harder to predict than volcanic eruptions. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the use of monitoring, prediction, protection and planning in reducing the effects of a tectonic hazard. (6 marks)
exit: Define 'secondary effect' and give one example.
Return to the big question: give two reasons why people live near tectonic hazards.
lessons.homework: Research the Pacific Tsunami Warning system or Japanese earthquake drills and write 100 words on how it reduces risk.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded sort cards for effects and responses. EAL: bilingual keyword mat. Stretch: judge which strategy matters most for a low-income country and justify it.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Tectonic hazards (AQA 3.1.1.2)
lessons.title: Tectonic case studies: Nepal 2015 and Christchurch 2011 compared
lessons.bigQuestion: Does a country's wealth decide how much a tectonic disaster hurts?
objectives: Describe the causes, effects and responses of the 2015 Nepal earthquake (low-income country)
Describe the causes, effects and responses of the 2011 Christchurch earthquake (high-income country)
Compare the two events and explain the differences
successCriteria: All: state the place, date, magnitude and at least two effects for each earthquake
Most: compare responses using specific facts
Some: explain the differences by linking to levels of development, not only the size of the earthquake
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: comparing death tolls and magnitudes; Science: the energy of magnitude scales
lessons.smsc: Moral and social: solidarity with people in disaster, and the role of aid; understanding that suffering is not equal

keywords.def: the energy released by an earthquake, measured on the moment magnitude scale
when shaking turns wet ground into a liquid-like mud
a smaller earthquake that follows the main shock
a country with low average income and limited resources
a country with high average income and many resources

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four types of plate margin and one place for each.
State two primary effects of an earthquake.
State two ways of reducing the effects of earthquakes.

teach.heading: Case study: Nepal earthquake, 2015

timeline.label: 25 April 2015
timeline.text: Magnitude 7.8 earthquake; epicentre near Barpak, Gorkha district, about 80 km north-west of Kathmandu; shallow focus

timeline.label: Effects
timeline.text: About 9,000 killed and about 22,000 injured; over 500,000 homes destroyed (approx.); Dharahara Tower collapsed; avalanche on Everest killed 19

timeline.label: 12 May 2015
timeline.text: Major aftershock, magnitude 7.3, caused more deaths and landslides

timeline.label: Immediate response
timeline.text: Nepalese army, India, China, the UK and many NGOs; tents, food and rescue teams; remote villages cut off by landslides

timeline.label: Long term
timeline.text: National Reconstruction Authority set up; rebuilding slow; new building rules; tourism damaged

teach.note: Cause: Nepal lies on the collision margin of the Indian and Eurasian plates. Nepal is a low-income country: dense hill villages built of stone and mud brick, little earthquake design, and few resources for rescue. Teach the figures as approximate and say so; the exact death toll differs by source. Ask: why did it take days for help to reach some villages? (Landslides blocked mountain roads; few helicopters; poor infrastructure.) Treat with sensitivity: this was a real tragedy, and many people were bereaved.

teach.heading: Case study: Christchurch earthquake, 2011

timeline.label: 22 February 2011
timeline.text: Magnitude 6.3; focus shallow (about 5 km); epicentre about 10 km from the city centre; New Zealand sits on the Pacific and Australian plate margin

timeline.label: Effects
timeline.text: 185 people killed (115 in the CTV building collapse); about 100,000 homes damaged; liquefaction flooded streets; city centre cordoned off

timeline.label: Economic cost
timeline.text: Around NZ$40 billion (approx.), mostly insured

timeline.label: Immediate response
timeline.text: Local and international rescue teams; shelters; water and power restored within days to weeks

timeline.label: Long term
timeline.text: Insurance paid for rebuilding; new building rules; city centre rebuilt over a decade

teach.note: Link to magnitude: this earthquake was smaller (6.3) than Nepal's (7.8) but caused huge damage because it was shallow and near a city. New Zealand is a high-income country with strong building codes, so most people survived and most losses were insured. Note the 115 deaths in one building which had structural problems. Ask: what do the deaths in Christchurch tell us about the limits of wealth? Check dates and figures before the lesson; they are accurate to the best of the author's knowledge but approximations are marked approx.

teach.heading: Compare the two events

head: Feature
Nepal 2015 (LIC)
Christchurch 2011 (HIC)
rows: Slow in remote areas; relied on foreign help
Fast; trained local teams plus international teams
Funded largely by insurance; city rebuilt

teach.note: Ask pupils to look for the surprise: the bigger earthquake had the bigger toll, but Christchurch's smaller quake still caused heavy damage. Conclude: magnitude matters but development is the key difference in deaths and recovery. Do not say poorer countries have no capacity: Nepal had good community response. Remind pupils that the exam wants place-specific facts to be used inside an explanation.

teach.heading: Skill: a comparison paragraph

model.problem: Compare the effects of an earthquake in a low-income country and a high-income country. (4 marks)
steps: Compare, not list: use 'whereas', 'but' and 'however'.
Use a fact from each place: about 9,000 deaths in Nepal and 185 in Christchurch.
Give the reason: weaker buildings and slower emergency help in Nepal.
Close with the main similarity or difference as a judgement.
model.answer: The 2015 Nepal earthquake killed about 9,000 people, whereas the 2011 Christchurch earthquake killed 185. This is because Nepal is a low-income country with weaker buildings and fewer rescue resources, while New Zealand has strict building codes and trained rescue teams. However, both events destroyed many homes.

teach.note: I do. Underline the comparative words. Pupils often write two separate paragraphs and miss the comparison marks. Show how to join facts with 'whereas'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Christchurch had a smaller magnitude than Nepal. What is the best explanation for its large damage?
options: The earthquake was shallow and close to a city
check.why: B is correct: shallow focus and nearness to people raise damage. A, C and D are false for New Zealand. Pupils choosing A have stereotyped wealth.

teach.note: Answer: B. Use it to show that the nature of the hazard interacts with human factors.

practice: Create a fact file for each earthquake: date, magnitude, cause, two primary effects, two secondary effects, two responses.
Mark each fact as 'nature of the hazard' or 'level of development'.
independent: Core: Give two primary effects of the earthquake in your chosen LIC or HIC case study. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how the responses to the two earthquakes differed. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'The wealth of a country is the most important factor in the damage caused by earthquakes.' Using two case studies, how far do you agree? (9 marks)
exit: Name one effect and one response for Nepal 2015.
Return to the big question: write one sentence on wealth and one on magnitude.
lessons.homework: Complete a one-page revision sheet on your two case studies with a checklist of place facts, then self-test with the table covered.
lessons.send: SEND: fact cards with highlighted numbers. EAL: key vocabulary and sentence stems for comparing. Stretch: add Tohoku 2011, Japan, as a third example and discuss the role of tsunamis.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Weather hazards in the UK (AQA 3.1.1.3, UK strand; tropical storms are taught in the existing Unit 1 lessons)
lessons.title: UK weather hazards and extreme weather: the July 2022 heatwave
lessons.bigQuestion: Is the UK's weather becoming more extreme?
objectives: Outline the main UK weather hazards
Use evidence to judge whether UK weather is becoming more extreme
Describe the impacts of, and management response to, the July 2022 heatwave
successCriteria: All: name four UK weather hazards and one impact of each
Most: use two pieces of evidence to say whether weather is becoming more extreme
Some: assess how well the 2022 heatwave was managed
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading record temperature data; Science: heat and health
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the vulnerable in extreme weather, neighbour by neighbour

keywords.def: weather events well outside the normal range, such as record heat or rain
a prolonged period of unusually hot weather
a long period with much less rainfall than normal
when water covers land that is normally dry
the UK's national weather service that issues weather warnings

starter: Say Bismillah. What is the difference between weather and climate?
Name the two types of climate change cause: natural and human. Give one of each.
Define 'risk'.

teach.heading: UK weather hazards

head: Hazard
Typical season
Example impact
rows: Autumn and winter, also summer storms
Power cuts, fallen trees, ferry and train disruption
Health risks, wildfires, crop and water shortages
Travel chaos, schools closed, risk to the elderly

teach.note: Brainstorm first. This slide covers the outline of UK hazards in the spec; tropical storms have already been taught in this course, so do not repeat. Emphasise that the UK's temperate maritime climate rarely has extremes, so the country is not well prepared: roads and homes are built for cool, wet weather, not 40 degrees. Ask: why does a small amount of snow cause such disruption? (Little equipment and planning, because it is rare.)

teach.heading: Evidence: record UK temperatures

timeline.text: Cheltenham: 37.1 °C (approx.)
Faversham, Kent: 38.5 °C
Cambridge Botanic Garden: 38.7 °C
Coningsby, Lincolnshire: 40.3 °C, the first time 40 °C was recorded in the UK

teach.note: Ask pupils what the pattern suggests (records are being broken more often). Add other evidence: the Met Office reports that the UK's warmest years have mostly occurred since 2002 (teacher to check the current list); winter 2013 to 2014 was the wettest on record for England and Wales (approx. record series from 1766); Storm Desmond in December 2015 set a new UK 24-hour rainfall record (about 341 mm at Honister Pass, Cumbria). Counter-point for balance: weather varies naturally, and a few records do not prove a trend. Climate scientists link the pattern to climate change.

teach.heading: Case study: July 2022 heatwave

head: Feature
Detail
rows: 18 to 19 July 2022; England worst; 40.3 °C at Coningsby on 19 July
First ever Red warning for extreme heat from the Met Office
Heat-related deaths estimated at about 3,000 for summer 2022 in England (approx.)
Rail speed limits and cancellations; Luton Airport runway damage; fires in London, e.g. Wennington
Warnings; advice to stay indoors and check on elderly neighbours; hosepipe bans later in summer; drought declared in many areas in August

teach.note: Ask pupils which impacts are primary and which secondary. Cause: a plume of hot air from Spain and the Sahara pushed north under a high-pressure system. Management happens before (forecasts and warnings), during (advice, services) and after (drought measures, review). Ask: how well prepared was the UK? Pupils can use evidence both ways. Death estimates vary by report; check the current UKHSA figure before teaching and say 'about'.

teach.heading: Skill: use evidence for a view

model.problem: 'UK weather is becoming more extreme.' Use evidence to support this view. (3 marks)
steps: Make a claim: records are being broken.
Add a precise piece of evidence: 40.3 °C recorded in July 2022, higher than the 2019 record of 38.7 °C.
Link evidence to the claim: higher records more often suggest greater extremes.
Add one more piece of evidence or a balance point.
model.answer: The evidence suggests that UK weather is becoming more extreme. In July 2022 the UK recorded 40.3 °C for the first time, higher than the previous record of 38.7 °C in 2019, which shows temperature records are being broken. In winter 2013 to 2014 England and Wales also had record rainfall.

teach.note: I do. Show how a number turns a vague statement into a mark. Stress that evidence must be specific. Invite a balance point: a few records do not prove a trend.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the best example of a long-term response to a heatwave?
options: A Red warning from the Met Office
A review of rail networks to cope with higher temperatures
check.why: C is long-term planning. A and D are immediate; B is a short-term management measure during drought.

teach.note: Answer: C. This links to the same vocabulary in tectonics: immediate versus long-term.

practice: List UK weather hazards and for each give one economic and one social impact.
Make a spider diagram of the impacts of the 2022 heatwave, using different colours for primary and secondary.
independent: Core: Give two UK weather hazards. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain two impacts of a recent UK extreme weather event you have studied. (4 marks)
Stretch: Assess the evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme. (6 marks)
exit: State one piece of evidence that UK temperatures are changing.
Return to the big question: give one reason for and one reason against.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word summary: 'How did the UK respond to the July 2022 heatwave?' Include at least two facts.
lessons.send: SEND: highlighted fact cards and sentence stems. EAL: weather vocabulary with pictures. Stretch: compare the 2022 heatwave with a flood event such as Storm Desmond.

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Climate change (AQA 3.1.1.4)
lessons.title: Climate change: the evidence and the causes
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know the climate is changing, and what is causing it?
objectives: Describe evidence for climate change from the Quaternary to the present
Explain natural causes of climate change: orbital changes, volcanic eruptions and solar output
Explain human causes: fossil fuels, agriculture and deforestation
successCriteria: All: give three pieces of evidence and name natural and human causes
Most: explain how the greenhouse effect is enhanced by human activity
Some: judge the relative importance of natural and human causes of recent warming
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the greenhouse effect; Maths: reading line graphs
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship (khalifah) of the Earth and responsibility to future generations; avoiding waste and excess

keywords.def: the geological period of the last 2.6 million years, with repeated ice ages
natural warming of the Earth because gases trap heat in the atmosphere
extra warming caused by human greenhouse gas emissions
coal, oil and gas formed from ancient plants and animals
the removal of forests on a large scale

starter: Say Bismillah. Name one UK weather hazard and its impact.
Where do volcanoes occur? (Link: volcanic ash is one natural cause of climate change.)
What is the difference between weather and climate?

teach.heading: Climate in the Quaternary

timeline.label: 2.6 million years ago
timeline.text: Start of the Quaternary: cycles of cold glacials and warm interglacials

timeline.label: About 20,000 years ago
timeline.text: Last glacial maximum: ice sheets covered much of the UK

timeline.label: About 11,700 years ago
timeline.text: Warm Holocene begins; temperatures rise

timeline.label: 1850 to 1900
timeline.text: Starting point for modern comparison (pre-industrial)

timeline.label: 2011 to 2020
timeline.text: About 1.1 °C warmer than 1850 to 1900 (IPCC); carbon dioxide above 410 ppm

teach.note: Make the point that the climate has always changed naturally, so the question is why it is changing so fast now. Pupils should notice the direction of recent change. Keep figures as approximations: the IPCC reports the 2011 to 2020 decade about 1.1 °C above 1850 to 1900, and carbon dioxide concentrations above 410 parts per million (they were about 280 before the Industrial Revolution). Teacher to check the latest reported figures before teaching.

teach.heading: Evidence for climate change

head: Evidence
What it shows
rows: Trapped air bubbles show past carbon dioxide and temperature over hundreds of thousands of years
Thermometer records since about 1850 show recent warming
Arctic sea ice and most glaciers are shrinking
Risen about 20 cm since 1900 (IPCC); warming water expands, ice melts
Show past vegetation and climate over thousands of years

teach.note: Ask how scientists find out about climate 100,000 years ago (there were no thermometers). Ice cores are the best-known evidence: layers of ice trap air from the past. Point out limits: some evidence is indirect (pollen) and has uncertainty. For recent change, direct measurements are available. Pupils should name the evidence and say what it shows, not just list it.

teach.heading: Natural and human causes

left.title: Natural causes
points: Orbital changes: tilt and orbit shape vary over tens of thousands of years
Volcanic eruptions: ash and sulphur dioxide block sunlight and cool the Earth
Solar output: variations in the Sun's energy change warming slightly

right.title: Human causes
points: Burning fossil fuels in power, transport and industry releases carbon dioxide
Agriculture: cattle and rice produce methane; fertilisers produce nitrous oxide
Deforestation: fewer trees absorb carbon dioxide; burning releases it

teach.note: Ask which group explains the speed of recent warming. Natural causes work slowly, over thousands of years, so cannot explain the rapid rise since 1850; scientists point to human emissions. Mention Mount Pinatubo, 1991, which cooled the Earth for a couple of years. Misconception: the ozone hole causes global warming; it is a separate problem.

teach.heading: The enhanced greenhouse effect
cycle: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface
Earth releases heat as infrared radiation
Greenhouse gases absorb some and send it back
Burning fuels adds extra gases
More heat trapped: global temperature rises
teach.note: Run through the cycle. Stress that the greenhouse effect is natural and needed; without it the Earth would be too cold for life. The enhanced effect is the problem. Ask pupils to circle the step humans change.

teach.heading: Skill: explain a cause

model.problem: Explain how human activities may be causing global warming. (4 marks)
steps: Name the activity: burning fossil fuels.
Explain the process: it releases carbon dioxide into the air.
Link to warming: more greenhouse gas traps more heat.
Add a second activity: deforestation reduces the carbon dioxide absorbed.
model.answer: Burning fossil fuels in power stations and cars releases carbon dioxide. This greenhouse gas traps more heat in the atmosphere, which raises global temperatures. Deforestation also contributes because fewer trees are left to absorb carbon dioxide.

teach.note: I do. Each mark is a link in a chain: activity, process, result. Highlight the verbs. Common error: saying pollution makes holes in the atmosphere. Correct this.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which piece of evidence shows climate over the last 800,000 years?
check.why: Ice cores contain trapped air from thousands of years ago. Thermometer records only go back to about 1850.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Label the stages of the greenhouse effect on a diagram.
Sort causes into natural or human: volcanic ash, cattle farming, solar output, burning coal, orbit changes, deforestation.
independent: Core: Give two natural causes of climate change. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how deforestation contributes to climate change. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the claim that recent climate change is caused entirely by human activity. (6 marks)
exit: Name two types of evidence for climate change.
Return to the big question: give one piece of evidence and one cause.
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled infographic of the greenhouse effect. Add three facts on evidence and cite the source.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn greenhouse effect diagram to label. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: explain why scientists can be confident the recent warming is mainly human-caused.

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Climate change (AQA 3.1.1.4)
lessons.title: Climate change: effects, mitigation and adaptation
lessons.bigQuestion: Should we focus on stopping climate change or on adapting to it?
objectives: Give an overview of effects of climate change on people and the environment
Explain mitigation: alternative energy, carbon capture, tree planting and international agreements
Explain adaptation: changing farming, managing water supply and reducing risk from rising sea levels
successCriteria: All: give two effects and one mitigation and one adaptation strategy
Most: explain how each strategy works
Some: evaluate mitigation against adaptation and make a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: renewable energy and carbon capture; Economics: costs and benefits
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship, and fairness to countries that contribute least but suffer most

keywords.def: action to reduce the causes of climate change
action to cope with the effects of climate change
trapping carbon dioxide from power stations and storing it underground
energy from sources that do not run out, such as wind and solar
the increase in average sea level as ice melts and oceans warm

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two human causes of climate change.
What is the greenhouse effect?
Give one piece of evidence that the climate is changing.

teach.heading: Effects of climate change

head: Area
People
Environment
rows: Coastal flooding, loss of land and homes
Melting glaciers, ice sheets; rising sea level
More heatwaves, floods and droughts; damage to homes
Changing rainfall and more extreme storms
Coral bleaching; species moving or dying out

teach.note: Do not present all effects as certain at every location: some places may get wetter, others drier. Ask pupils which groups are most vulnerable: low-lying nations such as Bangladesh and Pacific islands. Link to earlier lessons on capacity to cope. Teach the term 'overview': the spec wants a broad picture, not a case study.

teach.heading: Two responses

left.title: Mitigation: tackle the cause
points: Alternative energy: wind, solar, nuclear
Carbon capture: store emissions underground
Planting trees: absorb carbon dioxide
International agreements: Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015) set emissions targets

right.title: Adaptation: cope with the effects
points: Farming: drought-resistant crops, changing planting dates
Water supply: reservoirs, rainwater harvesting, reducing waste
Sea-level risk: sea walls, raised homes, barriers such as the Thames Barrier
Flood warnings and shelters

teach.note: Make the distinction crisp: mitigation attacks the cause, adaptation lives with the effect. Pupils swap them regularly. Paris Agreement 2015: nations aim to keep warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C. Ask for strengths and limits of each: mitigation needs cooperation between countries; adaptation is local and quick but does not stop the cause. Thames Barrier opened in 1982 to protect London from tidal surges.

teach.heading: Strategy evaluation

head: Strategy
Strength
Weakness
rows: Costly to build; some depend on weather
Allows continued use of fossil fuels with fewer emissions
Expensive; storage sites needed; not yet widespread
Slow; trees take years to grow
Cost; does not stop climate change

teach.note: Use this table as a bank of evaluation material: strength and weakness for each. Ask pupils which strategy they would choose if they were an adviser to a low-income country, and why. Stress there is no single right answer; the mark is for the reasoning and the judgement. Weigh cost, speed, effectiveness and fairness.

teach.heading: Skill: a balanced judgement

model.problem: Evaluate the success of mitigation and adaptation as ways of managing climate change. (6 marks, outline)
steps: Argument for mitigation: it addresses the cause so benefits are long-term and global.
Argument against: it needs international agreement and is slow to deliver results.
Argument for adaptation: it protects people now, for example flood barriers.
Judgement: both are needed; mitigation is more important over time but adaptation protects the vulnerable now.
model.answer: Mitigation, such as the Paris Agreement, tackles the cause and so could benefit everyone in the long term, but it needs countries to cooperate. Adaptation, such as raised homes in coastal areas, protects people straight away but does not stop climate change. Overall a combination is best because mitigation reduces future risk and adaptation protects people now.

teach.note: I do. Use the structure: argue, counter, judge. Students find the judgement hardest, so give a stem: 'Overall, ... is more important because ...'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is an example of adaptation?
options: Building flood barriers in a coastal town
check.why: C copes with sea-level rise. A, B and D reduce the causes.

teach.note: Answer: C. If a pupil chooses B, ask whether planting trees stops a flood or removes carbon dioxide.

practice: Sort strategies into mitigation or adaptation: solar farm, drought-resistant crops, tree planting, sea wall, Paris Agreement, rainwater harvesting.
Write one strength and one weakness for each of carbon capture and sea walls.
independent: Core: State the difference between mitigation and adaptation. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how people can adapt to the risk of sea-level rise. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'Mitigation is more important than adaptation.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Name one mitigation and one adaptation strategy.
Return to the big question: take a side and give one reason.
lessons.homework: Write a letter to a politician explaining which climate strategy you would prioritise, with two reasons. About 150 words.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards and sentence frame 'Mitigation is... whereas adaptation is...'. EAL: key terms in home language. Stretch: research one country's climate adaptation plan.

lessons.unit: Unit 5: Ecosystems (AQA 3.1.2.1)
lessons.title: Ecosystems: food webs, nutrient cycling, biomes and a UK woodland
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to a whole ecosystem when just one part changes?
objectives: Explain producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains, food webs and nutrient cycling
Show how changing one component affects the balance of the system
Describe the distribution of the main global biomes and a small-scale UK ecosystem
successCriteria: All: label a food chain and name the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers
Most: explain the effect of changing one part of a food web or nutrient cycle
Some: use a case study to show interdependence in an ecosystem and link biomes to climate
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: food webs, photosynthesis and decay
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and moral: balance (mizan) in creation; our responsibility not to disturb it carelessly

keywords.def: a community of living things and the non-living environment they interact with
an organism that makes its own food, such as a plant
an organism that eats other living things
an organism that breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the soil
linked food chains showing feeding relationships
a large-scale ecosystem with similar climate, plants and animals

starter: Say Bismillah. What do plants need for photosynthesis?
What is a food chain? Give an example of three links.
What happens to leaves when they fall and rot?

teach.heading: Parts of an ecosystem
bullets: Producers make food by photosynthesis, such as oak trees and grass.
Consumers eat plants or animals, such as mice and owls.
Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead matter.
Non-living parts: climate, soil, water and rock.
teach.note: Start from a pupil's local park or woodland and have them name living and non-living parts. Draw a woodland food chain: oak leaf, caterpillar, blue tit, sparrowhawk. A food web links many chains. Stress arrows show the flow of energy, pointing from the eaten to the eater: the common mistake is arrows pointing the wrong way. Ecosystems vary in size: a pond is small-scale, a biome is large-scale.

teach.heading: Nutrient cycle in a woodland
cycle: Trees take up nutrients from the soil
Nutrients are stored in leaves, branches and trunk
Leaf fall adds litter to the ground
Decomposers break down the litter
Nutrients return to the soil
teach.note: In the Gersmehl model nutrients move between three stores: biomass, litter and soil. Ask which store is largest in a temperate woodland (soil and litter hold a lot) compared with a rainforest (biomass). This idea returns in the rainforest lesson. Misconception: soils contain endless nutrients; if the cycle is broken, for example by removing the litter or cutting the trees, the nutrients are lost. Link to mizan: the system works because each part does its job.

teach.heading: Skill: explain a change in a food web

model.problem: A pond food web includes algae, water fleas, small fish and herons. Pollution kills most of the water fleas. Explain the effect on the pond. (4 marks)
steps: Direct effect: the small fish lose a food source, so they decline.
Knock-on effect: with fewer small fish, herons have less to eat.
Opposite effect: algae, no longer eaten, may increase and block light.
State that one change disrupts balance through the whole web.
model.answer: If water fleas die, small fish have less food so their numbers fall. This means herons have less to eat and may move away. Algae are eaten less so they may grow rapidly and block light, which shows that changing one part upsets the balance of the whole ecosystem.

teach.note: I do. Show how arrows in the food web give the chain of reasoning. Ask: what would happen if the herons were removed instead? Pupils practise predicting both increases and decreases; many only predict decreases.

teach.heading: Global biomes

head: Biome
Location
Climate and plants
rows: Hot and wet all year; dense evergreen forest
Either side of rainforests (e.g. East Africa)
Warm with wet and dry seasons; grass and scattered trees
About 20 to 30 degrees north and south (e.g. Sahara)
Mild, rain all year; trees lose leaves in winter
Very cold; low plants, frozen ground

teach.note: Show a world map. Pupils colour in biomes to see that climate controls the biome: temperature and rainfall decide which plants can grow, and plants decide which animals live there. Ask: why are deserts found near 30 degrees north and south? (Sinking dry air, linked to atmospheric circulation covered earlier.) Boreal coniferous forest (taiga) may also be mentioned between the temperate forests and tundra.

teach.heading: Case study: a UK woodland, e.g. Epping Forest (or a local wood)
teach.note: Choose a named woodland: use Epping Forest (Essex and Greater London) as the example or the teacher's local woodland or a pond if fieldwork has been done there. Use the table to talk about interdependence: the oak supports hundreds of insect species, which feed birds, which feed predators such as tawny owls and sparrowhawks. Fungi and bacteria recycle leaf litter. Ask what would happen if deer numbers soared (grazing could remove the bluebells and young trees). Check any named site facts before teaching; the table is general.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: In a food web, what do the arrows show?
options: The direction of energy flow, from the food to the eater
check.why: Arrows point from the organism being eaten to the one that eats it, showing energy transfer.

teach.note: Answer: B. A common error is to point the arrow from the predator to the prey.

practice: Draw a food web for a woodland using at least six organisms and label producers, consumers and decomposers.
Predict what happens if rabbits are removed from your web.
independent: Core: Define the term 'decomposer'. (1 mark) Give one example. (1 mark)
Extend: Explain how a change in one part of an ecosystem affects the others. (4 marks)
Stretch: Using a named UK ecosystem, explain how the plants, animals and soil depend on each other. (6 marks)
exit: Which biome is found near the equator?
Return to the big question: give one example of a change causing a chain of effects.
lessons.homework: Draw a nutrient cycle for a woodland or pond and explain what would happen if all the decomposers died. About 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn food web with cut-out organisms to arrange. EAL: labelled pictures for producer/consumer/decomposer. Stretch: link biome distribution to atmospheric circulation and ocean currents.

lessons.unit: Unit 6: Tropical rainforests (AQA 3.1.2.2)
lessons.title: Tropical rainforests: climate, interdependence and adaptation
lessons.bigQuestion: How can the most species-rich ecosystem on Earth grow on poor soil?
objectives: Describe the physical characteristics of tropical rainforests
Explain how climate, soil, plants, animals and water interrelate
Explain plant and animal adaptations and why biodiversity is so high
successCriteria: All: describe the climate and the layers of the rainforest
Most: explain how the nutrient cycle and the soil are connected to the climate and plants
Some: explain adaptations and link them to the competition for light, food and survival
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: adaptation and photosynthesis
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the diversity and complexity of creation as signs for those who reflect

keywords.def: the variety of plant and animal species in a place
the dense layer of treetops, about 25 to 45 m above the ground
the tallest trees that rise above the canopy
a plant that grows on another plant, using it for light without harming it
a feature that helps an organism survive in its environment

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the biome near the equator and two features of its climate.
Explain what a decomposer does.
Describe what happens to nutrients when a leaf falls.

teach.heading: Climate and location

head: Feature
Tropical rainforest
rows: Within about 10 degrees of the equator: Amazon, Congo, Southeast Asia
About 26 to 28 °C all year (approx.); little seasonal change
Over 2,000 mm a year; rain nearly every day
Evergreen trees in layers; dense growth

teach.note: Link the climate to the equatorial low-pressure belt: the Sun is high, air rises, and convection rain falls daily. Use Manaus, Brazil as a data point if the class has done climate graphs: about 27 °C and about 2,300 mm rain a year (approx.). Ask pupils to describe, not explain, and then ask them to explain why the growth is so fast (heat, water, light all year).

teach.heading: Interdependence: climate to soil
cycle: Hot, wet climate gives rapid plant growth
Dead leaves fall and decompose in weeks
Nutrients are taken up quickly by shallow roots
Most nutrients are held in plants, not soil
Soil is thin and nutrient-poor; heavy rain washes nutrients out
teach.note: Stress the paradox: lush forest on poor soil. The forest survives because the nutrients are recycled so fast they do not stay in the soil. This also explains why cleared forest soon becomes infertile, which we use in the next lesson. Ask pupils which store in the Gersmehl model is largest here (biomass) and which is smallest (litter, since it decays so fast, and soil).

teach.heading: Adaptations

left.title: Plants
points: Drip tips shed rainwater
Buttress roots support tall trees on thin soil
Epiphytes grow on branches to reach light
Lianas climb up trees using them for support

right.title: Animals
points: Camouflage, such as sloths covered in algae
Warning colours, such as poison dart frogs
Long limbs and prehensile tails for climbing
Many are nocturnal or live in specific layers

teach.note: Ask pupils to link each adaptation to the problem it solves: waterlogged leaves, lack of light, predators. Biodiversity: over half of the world's land plant and animal species may live in rainforests (a commonly quoted estimate; treat as approx.). Competition for light and food drives specialisation, and niches in each layer create a huge range of species. Emphasise to pupils that adaptation takes place over generations; individual animals do not adapt in their lifetimes.

teach.heading: Skill: explain an adaptation

model.problem: Explain how one adaptation helps a plant to survive in a rainforest. (3 marks)
steps: Name the adaptation: buttress roots.
Say what it does: they spread out at the base of tall trees.
Link to the problem: the soil is thin, so they stop the tree falling over.
model.answer: Many rainforest trees have buttress roots. These spread widely at the base of the trunk, so they give support in thin, shallow soil, which stops the tall trees falling over in heavy rain and wind.

teach.note: I do. Three marks means name, describe, explain. Pupils often just name the adaptation. Ask them to rehearse with drip tips: it lets heavy rain run off quickly so the leaf does not grow mould or break.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Why is the soil in a tropical rainforest often poor in nutrients?
options: Nutrients are quickly taken up by plants and washed out by heavy rain
check.why: Rapid recycling holds nutrients in biomass, and rainfall washes the surplus out. Decomposers are active, not absent.

teach.note: Answer: B. Pupils choosing C mix up cause and effect: decomposition is fast, which is why little litter builds up.

practice: Draw and label the layers of a rainforest with the typical height of each.
Match each adaptation to the problem it solves.
independent: Core: Describe the climate of a tropical rainforest. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how rainforest plants are adapted to the conditions. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain how climate, soils, plants and animals are interdependent in the rainforest. (6 marks)
exit: Name two adaptations of rainforest animals.
Return to the big question: summarise in one sentence why rainforest soil is poor.
lessons.homework: Create a labelled poster of a rainforest food web showing at least three adaptations.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-labelled rainforest layers diagram. EAL: pictures and bilingual labels for adaptations. Stretch: explain why biodiversity is greater in rainforests than in temperate forests.

lessons.unit: Unit 6: Tropical rainforests (AQA 3.1.2.2)
lessons.title: Deforestation in the Amazon: rates, causes and impacts
lessons.bigQuestion: Who gains and who loses when the rainforest is cleared?
objectives: Describe changing rates of deforestation in the Amazon, Brazil
Explain causes: farming, logging, road building, mineral extraction, energy and settlement
Assess the impacts on economic development, soil erosion and climate change
successCriteria: All: name three causes of deforestation and one impact
Most: use figures from the Amazon to describe changing rates and explain causes
Some: assess both benefits and costs and reach a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: costs, benefits and opportunity cost; Maths: describing change over time
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing short-term profit against the trust (amanah) we hold for future generations

keywords.def: the permanent removal of forest, mostly for farming, logging and building
raising cattle on large areas of cleared land
the removal of topsoil by wind or water
cutting only the most valuable trees
washing of nutrients out of the soil by rain

starter: Say Bismillah. Why is rainforest soil low in nutrients?
Describe one adaptation of a rainforest plant.
Name one human cause of climate change.

teach.heading: Changing rates: Brazilian Amazon

timeline.label: 1970s
timeline.text: Roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway open the forest to settlers and ranchers
Peak: about 27,800 km² cleared in one year (approx.)
Low: about 4,600 km² (approx.) after tougher enforcement and satellite monitoring
Rises again: about 13,000 km² (approx.)

timeline.label: Overall
timeline.text: About 17% of the Brazilian Amazon forest has been lost (approx.)

teach.note: Rates are a question of change over time; they are not constant, because policy and prices matter. Teach pupils to describe the trend with figures: falling by more than 80 per cent between 2004 and 2012, then rising again. Figures are annual estimates of the Brazilian space agency satellite programme and are approximate; teacher to check against the latest data. The 17 per cent is often quoted as an estimate for total loss of the Brazilian Amazon since the 1970s; label as approx.

teach.heading: Causes of deforestation

head: Cause
How it clears forest
rows: Largest cause in Brazil: forest cleared and burned for pasture
Soya and other crops grown for export and animal feed
Legal and illegal timber extraction; logging roads open the forest
Roads such as the BR-163 and the Trans-Amazonian Highway bring settlers
Iron ore and gold mines; hydroelectric dams such as Belo Monte flood forest
Poor farmers and growing towns clear land for housing and subsistence farming

teach.note: Ask pupils to rank causes by their importance. Note that some causes work together: roads allow loggers in; loggers allow ranchers in. Be fair: many people clearing land are poor families seeking a living, and also large companies. Check pupils' understanding by asking which causes are commercial and which are subsistence.

teach.heading: Soil erosion after clearance
cycle: Trees are removed
Bare soil is hit by heavy rain
Topsoil and nutrients are washed away
Rivers silt up; land loses fertility
Farms are abandoned and more forest is cleared
teach.note: Draw this on the board. The cycle shows why cleared land is often productive only for a few years, which pushes farmers to clear more. Link to the interdependence lesson: without trees there is no leaf litter and the nutrient cycle breaks. Ask: what other effects arise from silt in rivers? (Fish habitats are damaged.)

teach.heading: Impacts of deforestation

left.title: Benefits
points: Jobs and income from ranching, farming and mining
Exports bring money into Brazil
Roads and energy support development

right.title: Costs
points: Soil erosion and loss of fertility
Loss of habitats and species
Less carbon dioxide absorbed; burning releases it; less rainfall locally
Loss of homes and culture for indigenous peoples

teach.note: Ask for a view: whose benefits and whose costs? Link the climate impact: trees store carbon, so cutting and burning them adds carbon dioxide; fewer trees means less water released to the air (transpiration), so less rain may fall. The spec expects an assessment, which means weighing. Possible judgement: benefits are short-term and uneven; costs are long-term and global.

teach.heading: Skill: case-study paragraph

model.problem: Using the Amazon rainforest, explain two causes of deforestation. (4 marks)
steps: Cause 1 with detail: cattle ranching, where forest is burned for pasture in Brazil.
Explain why: beef is a valuable export, so there is strong demand for land.
Cause 2 with detail: roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway, opened in the 1970s.
Explain why: roads allow settlers, loggers and farmers into the forest.
model.answer: One cause is cattle ranching because large areas of forest in Brazil are burned for pasture and beef is a valuable export. Another cause is road building, as roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway let settlers and loggers enter the forest and clear land.

teach.note: I do. Case-study questions always need a named place and a place fact. Highlight the specific words. Pupils often write generic causes with no Amazon detail, and so lose marks.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Why does soil erosion increase after trees are cut down?
options: Roots hold soil and leaves shelter it from rain, and without them rain hits bare soil
check.why: Removing trees exposes soil and removes the roots that bind it, so heavy rain washes it away.

teach.note: Answer: A.

practice: Describe the trend in Amazon deforestation using the figures from 2004, 2012 and 2021.
Complete a table of causes with one Amazon fact for each.
independent: Core: State two causes of deforestation in the Amazon. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how deforestation can lead to soil erosion. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess the impacts of deforestation on people and the environment in a named rainforest area. (6 marks)
exit: State one economic benefit of deforestation and one cost.
Return to the big question: name one group who gain and one who lose.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word letter from a rancher and from an indigenous leader about deforestation to compare views.
lessons.send: SEND: causes sorting cards with Amazon facts. EAL: key terms with visuals. Stretch: use rate figures to calculate the percentage fall between 2004 and 2012.

lessons.unit: Unit 6: Tropical rainforests (AQA 3.1.2.2)
lessons.title: Why the rainforest matters and how to manage it sustainably
lessons.bigQuestion: Can the rainforest be used without being destroyed?
objectives: Explain the value of rainforests to people and the environment
Describe sustainable management strategies: selective logging, conservation, ecotourism, hardwood agreements and debt reduction
Evaluate which strategies are most effective in the Amazon
successCriteria: All: give two reasons why rainforests are valuable and name two strategies
Most: explain how each strategy helps to protect the forest
Some: evaluate strategies and make a justified recommendation
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: debt and trade; Science: carbon stores
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship and justice for indigenous peoples; balancing needs of the poor and the planet

keywords.def: using resources so they will still be available to future generations
protecting and looking after nature
tourism that protects the environment and benefits local people
an agreement to buy only timber from sustainable sources
cancelling debt in return for protecting the environment

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three causes of deforestation.
What is soil erosion?
Give one benefit and one cost of deforestation.

teach.heading: Why rainforests matter

left.title: People
points: Homes and culture of indigenous peoples
Food, timber, rubber, medicines and nuts
Jobs and tourism income
Help regulate rainfall

right.title: Environment
points: Home to about half of the world's species (approx.)
Store large amounts of carbon
Protect soil and water supplies
Release water vapour that affects the climate

teach.note: Ask pupils which value matters most to local people and which matters to the world. Emphasise that carbon storage gives the forest global value: when it is burned, carbon dioxide is released. Many modern medicines were originally developed from plants. Take care with statistics: do not claim rainforests are the 'lungs of the Earth', which is misleading as the forest uses most of the oxygen it produces.

teach.heading: Sustainable management strategies

head: Strategy
How it works
Strength
Weakness
rows: Only mature trees cut; canopy and young trees left
Reserves and indigenous territories protected by law
Visitors pay to see forest; money supports local people
Gives forest a value without clearing
Can damage if too many visit
Countries buy only timber from certified sources
Debt cancelled in return for protecting forest
Reduces pressure to sell forest resources

teach.note: Take each strategy and check what it does; the weakness column prepares pupils for evaluation. Debt-for-nature swaps began in 1987 when a conservation group bought part of Bolivia's debt. Brazil's protected areas and indigenous territories now cover a large share of the Amazon (check the current percentage before teaching). The Amazon Fund, set up in 2008 and supported by Norway and Germany, pays for forest protection. Keep the notes brief and focus on the exam skill.

teach.heading: Skill: evaluate sustainable management

model.problem: Evaluate the effectiveness of ecotourism and conservation in protecting the Amazon rainforest. (6 marks, outline)
steps: Ecotourism: gives income to local people and so reduces the need to clear land.
Limit: too many tourists damage trails and wildlife, and income is small compared with ranching.
Conservation: protected areas legally prevent clearance.
Limit and judgement: protected areas need enforcement; overall conservation is stronger but needs local income from ecotourism.
model.answer: Ecotourism gives local people an income without cutting trees, but the money is small compared with cattle ranching. Conservation areas protect the forest by law, but only if the law is enforced. Overall conservation is more effective, though it works best when local people also benefit from ecotourism.

teach.note: I do. Pupils must show a judgement and a reason. Remind them to name the Amazon in their answer. In 6-mark questions explanations should be developed, not just listed.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which strategy rewards a country for protecting forest by reducing what it owes?
check.why: Debt reduction (a debt-for-nature swap) cancels debt in return for conservation.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Complete the strategies table with a strength and weakness for each.
Rank the strategies from most to least effective and explain your choice.
independent: Core: Give two reasons why rainforests are valuable. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how selective logging can be sustainable. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the success of sustainable management strategies in a named rainforest area. (6 marks)
exit: State one strategy to manage rainforest sustainably and one weakness.
Return to the big question: answer yes or no and give a reason.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word proposal for a sustainable use of the rainforest to present to a council.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-filled table with cloze gaps. EAL: simple glossary with pictures. Stretch: evaluate how the Amazon Fund works and its limits.

lessons.unit: Unit 7: Cold environments (AQA 3.1.2.4; OPTION: hot deserts OR cold environments. Hot deserts are already taught in the existing Y10 Unit 2 lessons, so these cold-environment lessons are for classes or pupils taking that option)
lessons.title: Cold environments: tundra climate, permafrost and adaptation
lessons.bigQuestion: How can anything live where the ground is frozen for most of the year?
objectives: Describe the physical characteristics of the Arctic tundra
Explain links between climate, permafrost, soils, plants, animals and people
Explain plant and animal adaptations and why biodiversity is low
successCriteria: All: describe the climate and name three adaptations
Most: explain how permafrost affects soil, water and vegetation
Some: explain why cold environments are fragile and slow to recover
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: heat, freezing and adaptation
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on how life is sustained in even the harshest places

keywords.def: a cold treeless biome with low plants and frozen ground
ground that stays frozen for two or more years
the top layer of ground that thaws in summer
a feature that helps an organism to survive
easily damaged and slow to recover

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three biomes and one climate feature of each.
What is an adaptation? Give an example from the rainforest.
Why is biodiversity high in the rainforest?

teach.heading: Tundra location and climate

head: Feature
Arctic tundra
rows: North of the tree line, near the Arctic Circle: northern Alaska, Canada, Russia, Scandinavia
Winter below -30 °C is common; summer mean about 4 to 10 °C
Less than 250 mm a year, mostly snow: a cold desert
Up to 24 hours in summer and almost none in winter

teach.note: Use Utqiaġvik (Barrow), Alaska as a data point if you have a climate graph: an annual mean of around -12 °C and about 110 mm of precipitation (approx.). Explain that polar air is cold and dry and sinks, so little precipitation falls. The Antarctic is a polar desert and a different cold environment: for these lessons the case study is the Arctic tundra of Alaska, with Antarctica used in the third lesson.

teach.heading: Linked system
bullets: Cold climate keeps ground frozen as permafrost.
In summer the thin active layer thaws but cannot drain downwards.
Boggy, waterlogged, thin and acidic soils support low plants.
Few plants support few animals, so food chains are short.
teach.note: Draw a cross-section: active layer on top, permafrost beneath, which may be hundreds of metres deep (up to about 600 m at Prudhoe Bay, approx.). Water cannot drain through frozen ground, so the surface is marshy in summer. Ask pupils to say how people fit in: traditionally Inuit and Iñupiat hunting, fishing and herding. Link to the nutrient cycle: decay is slow in the cold, so nutrients are locked in dead matter. Remind pupils that cause and effect must be given in order.

teach.heading: Adaptations

left.title: Plants
points: Low, ground-hugging growth avoids wind
Shallow roots above the permafrost
Dark, hairy leaves absorb and hold heat, such as Arctic willow
Fast flowering in 24-hour summer daylight

right.title: Animals
points: Thick fur and fat, such as polar bear and musk ox
Seasonal colour change, such as Arctic fox and Arctic hare
Migration, such as caribou and many birds
Hibernation or reducing activity in winter

teach.note: Connect each adaptation to a problem: wind, cold, short growing season, camouflage. Note that biodiversity is low compared with the rainforest: few species can cope. Many species are specialists, so food chains are short and simple: if the number of one species falls, others are heavily affected. This also makes the environment fragile and slow to recover from damage, since plants take decades to regrow.

teach.heading: Skill: explain linkages

model.problem: Explain how permafrost affects vegetation in the tundra. (3 marks)
steps: Permafrost stops water draining, so the ground is boggy in summer.
Roots cannot penetrate the frozen layer, so plants are shallow-rooted and small.
Therefore trees cannot grow and vegetation is low mosses, lichens and grasses.
model.answer: Permafrost is frozen ground that water cannot drain through, so the soil is waterlogged in summer. Roots cannot grow deep, so only small, shallow-rooted plants such as mosses and lichens survive, and trees cannot grow.

teach.note: I do. Make the chain explicit with 'so' and 'because'. Most pupils say 'it is cold so nothing grows', which is too vague for the marks.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: What is the active layer?
options: The top layer of soil that thaws in summer
A layer of ice on lakes
check.why: The active layer thaws in summer above the permafrost. Pupils choosing A confuse it with the permafrost itself.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Draw a labelled cross-section of tundra ground showing the active layer and permafrost.
Match each adaptation to the problem it solves.
independent: Core: Describe the climate of the tundra. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how animals are adapted to the tundra. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain how climate, permafrost, soil and vegetation are linked in the tundra. (6 marks)
exit: Define permafrost.
Return to the big question: give one animal and one plant adaptation.
lessons.homework: Make an adaptation fact-file for one Arctic animal and one plant, with a diagram.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled cross-section to complete. EAL: picture glossary with key terms. Stretch: compare adaptations of tundra and desert species.

lessons.unit: Unit 7: Cold environments (AQA 3.1.2.4; OPTION: hot deserts OR cold environments. Hot deserts are already taught in the existing Y10 Unit 2 lessons, so these cold-environment lessons are for classes or pupils taking that option)
lessons.title: Alaska's North Slope: opportunities and challenges of development
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it worth the effort to develop one of the coldest places on Earth?
objectives: Describe opportunities: mineral extraction, energy, fishing and tourism
Explain challenges: extreme temperatures, inaccessibility, and providing buildings and infrastructure
Use Alaska as a case study to show how technology overcomes challenges
successCriteria: All: give two opportunities and two challenges of developing a cold environment
Most: explain how permafrost thaw damages buildings and how engineers cope
Some: judge how successfully the Trans-Alaska Pipeline overcame the challenges
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: heat transfer and building design
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing economic benefit against care for the land and for local peoples

keywords.def: the Arctic area of northern Alaska, including Prudhoe Bay oil field
difficult to reach, because of terrain or climate
roads, pipelines, buildings and services needed for development
uneven ground that forms when ice-rich permafrost thaws
a long tube that moves oil or gas

starter: Say Bismillah. What is permafrost?
Describe two adaptations of tundra plants.
Why is biodiversity low in cold environments?

teach.heading: Opportunities and challenges

head: Area
Opportunity
Challenge
rows: Oil and gas, coal, gold; hydro power
Extreme cold stops machines; permafrost sinks drills and pipes
Rich fisheries, such as pollock, salmon and crab off Alaska
Short season; costly access; fragile environment
Thawing ground causes buildings to sink; frozen pipes; few roads

teach.note: Link each opportunity to its matching challenge so that pupils practise 'Opportunity... but challenge...'. Tourism is a growing industry in Alaska, but locations such as the North Slope are remote. Extreme temperatures go to about -40 °C; metal becomes brittle, batteries fail, workers are at risk of frostbite and hypothermia. Inaccessible: few roads, so supplies come by air or ice roads. The Dalton Highway, built in the 1970s, runs about 666 miles (about 1,070 km) from Fairbanks to Deadhorse.

teach.heading: Case study: Trans-Alaska Pipeline

timeline.text: Huge oil field found at Prudhoe Bay on the North Slope

timeline.label: 1974 to 1977
timeline.text: Pipeline built, about 1,300 km (800 miles) from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez on the south coast

timeline.label: Design
timeline.text: About half of it raised above ground on supports with heat pipes so oil heat does not melt the permafrost
Exxon Valdez oil spill in Prince William Sound; a tanker, not the pipeline, but a warning about risk

timeline.label: Today
timeline.text: Oil income funds Alaska; output falling; debate about further drilling

teach.note: Explain why the pipeline is raised: the oil is warm, and if it were buried in ice-rich permafrost it would melt the ground, which would sink and break the pipe. Heat pipes (thermosyphons) draw heat from the supports. The route zigzags to allow for expansion and earthquake movement and has raised sections for caribou migration. Pipeline distance is about 1,287 km (approx.); proportion raised is about half (approx.); check. Ask pupils to weigh economic gain against risk.

teach.heading: Building in permafrost
bullets: Heated buildings melt the ground and sink.
Buildings are raised on piles so air can flow under.
Pipes for water and sewage are insulated and kept above ground.
Gravel pads spread weight and insulate the ground.
teach.note: Explain that thawed ground becomes mud and structures can crack or tilt. Climate change is also thawing permafrost, causing roads and buildings to subside in many Arctic settlements. Ask why building costs in Alaska are far higher than elsewhere (materials flown in, special foundations, short building season).

teach.heading: Skill: explain a challenge and solution

model.problem: Explain why building in permafrost areas is difficult and how engineers overcome this. (4 marks)
steps: Problem: heat from buildings melts the frozen ground.
Result: the ground becomes soft and the building sinks or cracks.
Solution: buildings and pipelines are built on stilts so air circulates.
Explain why this works: the ground under them stays frozen.
model.answer: Heat from buildings can melt the permafrost so the ground turns to mud and buildings sink or crack. Engineers build on stilts so cold air can flow under and keep the ground frozen, and they raise pipelines for the same reason.

teach.note: I do. Pupils often mention only the problem. Show how to add the solution and why it works. Give an Alaska example: parts of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline are raised.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Why are parts of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline raised above the ground?
options: So hot oil does not melt the permafrost beneath
To protect it from earthquakes only
To make it easier to paint
check.why: The oil is warm, so a buried pipe would melt the ground, which would sink. Raising on supports with heat pipes keeps the ground frozen.

teach.note: Answer: B. It also lets caribou migrate beneath.

practice: Complete the opportunity-and-challenge table for a cold environment using two facts from Alaska.
Explain with a diagram why buildings on stilts do not melt permafrost.
independent: Core: Give two challenges of developing cold environments. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how technology has helped development in a named cold environment. (4 marks)
