Stretch: 'The opportunities of developing cold environments outweigh the challenges.' How far do you agree? Use a case study. (6 marks)
exit: Name one opportunity and one challenge in Alaska.
Return to the big question: give a view with one reason.
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word briefing to an oil company about the main risks of building a pipeline across permafrost.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled diagram of raised pipeline; cloze summary. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: research how climate warming now threatens infrastructure built on permafrost.

lessons.unit: Unit 7: Cold environments (AQA 3.1.2.4; OPTION: hot deserts OR cold environments. Hot deserts are already taught in the existing Y10 Unit 2 lessons, so these cold-environment lessons are for classes or pupils taking that option)
lessons.title: Wilderness, treaties and balancing development with conservation
lessons.bigQuestion: Who should decide what happens to the last wilderness places on Earth?
objectives: Explain the value of cold environments as wilderness
Explain why cold environments need protection
Evaluate technology, governments, treaties and conservation groups as ways to balance development and conservation
successCriteria: All: name two reasons cold environments are valuable and two ways of protecting them
Most: explain how the Antarctic Treaty and technology protect cold environments
Some: evaluate which approach is best
lessons.crossCurricular: Politics: international law and treaties; Science: polar research
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship; fairness between present and future generations and between nations

keywords.def: a large natural area little affected by people
protecting nature from damage
a formal agreement between countries
a 1959 agreement setting aside Antarctica for peaceful and scientific use
development that meets present needs without harming future generations

starter: Say Bismillah. State two opportunities in cold environments.
Why is infrastructure difficult to build on permafrost?
Define 'conservation'.

teach.heading: Value of cold environments

left.title: Why they matter
points: Wilderness: huge areas with few people
Habitats for polar bears, caribou, migrating birds
Scientific research: ice cores and climate data
Store carbon in frozen ground

right.title: Why they need protection
points: Oil spills and pipelines threaten wildlife
Tourism and ships bring waste and noise
Fragile: plants and animals recover slowly
Climate change is warming the Arctic faster than most places

teach.note: Draw out that value has several types: ecological, scientific, cultural (indigenous peoples) and aesthetic. Fragility is the key reason protection matters: damage lasts decades. The Arctic has warmed about two to four times faster than the global average in recent decades (approx. and varies by study; check). Ask pupils what 'wilderness' means to them and how it could be valued. Be careful not to imply no people live there: indigenous peoples have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years.

teach.heading: Strategies to balance development and conservation

head: Strategy
Example
Strength
Limit
rows: Raised pipelines; directional drilling reduces surface footprint
Cannot remove all risk; spills still happen
Protected areas in Alaska such as the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
Laws and policy change with governments
Antarctic Treaty 1959; Madrid Protocol 1991 bans mining
Needs countries to agree and comply

teach.note: Dates: the Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 and came into force in 1961; it sets Antarctica aside for peaceful use and science. The Madrid Protocol was signed in 1991 and took effect in 1998; it bans mineral resource activities, with a review possible from 2048 (check wording). The Arctic has no equivalent treaty because it is mostly ocean surrounded by eight countries; the Arctic Council discusses cooperation. Ask pupils to say which strategy is hardest to enforce.

teach.heading: Skill: balanced judgement

model.problem: 'International treaties are the best way to protect cold environments.' How far do you agree? (6 marks, outline)
steps: For: treaties bind many countries, such as the Antarctic Treaty and its mining ban.
Against: treaties depend on countries agreeing and they have no real police; the Arctic has no such treaty.
Alternative: technology and conservation groups work at a local level.
Judgement: treaties are most powerful where there are no residents, but several approaches are needed.
model.answer: Treaties such as the Antarctic Treaty are effective because they bind many countries to peaceful use and a ban on mining. However they only work if countries comply, and the Arctic has no equivalent. Technology and conservation groups help locally, so overall treaties are powerful but need to be combined with other strategies.

teach.note: I do. The judgement must answer the 'how far' question. Insist on one sentence starting 'Overall'. Encourage a named example, such as the Antarctic Treaty or Alaska's refuge, for specific marks.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which strategy did the 1991 Madrid Protocol use to protect Antarctica?
check.why: The Protocol bans mining and sets rules on waste and wildlife, with a review no earlier than 2048.

teach.note: Answer: A.

practice: Sort the strategies into technology, governments, treaties or conservation groups, with an example for each.
Debate: 'Should Alaska allow more oil drilling?' with two arguments each side.
independent: Core: Give two reasons why cold environments need protecting. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how a treaty can protect a cold environment. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate strategies for balancing development and conservation in a named cold environment. (6 marks)
exit: Name one treaty protecting a cold environment and one thing it does.
Return to the big question: write one sentence of your view.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word policy briefing recommending how to balance development and conservation in Alaska.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-completed strategies table with gaps. EAL: key terms in home language. Stretch: compare protection of the Arctic and Antarctic.

lessons.unit: Unit 8: UK physical landscapes (AQA 3.1.3.1)
lessons.title: Where are the UK's uplands, lowlands and major rivers?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do the north and west of the UK look so different from the south and east?
objectives: Locate the major upland and lowland areas of the UK
Locate the major river systems of the UK
Describe the pattern and link it to geology and the landscape studies that follow
successCriteria: All: name and locate three upland areas, three lowland areas and three rivers
Most: describe the pattern of relief using compass directions
Some: explain the pattern using rock type and glaciation
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths and skills: map reading, scale and height; Geology
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at the variety of landscapes within one small country; stewardship of the land

keywords.def: high ground, usually over 200 m, with steep slopes
low, flatter land, usually below 200 m
a river and all its tributaries
where a river begins
where a river meets the sea or a lake

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four countries of the United Kingdom and their capitals.
What is a river's source and mouth?
Name one UK mountain and one UK river you know.

teach.heading: Upland and lowland UK

left.title: Upland: north and west
points: Hard, old rocks such as granite and slate
Steep slopes, thin soils, high rainfall
Mostly sheep farming, forestry and tourism
Shaped by ice during the last ice age

right.title: Lowland: south and east
points: Softer, younger rocks such as clay, chalk and sandstone
Gentle slopes, deep soils, drier and warmer
Arable farming, towns and cities
Many main rivers flow slowly across it

teach.note: Show a relief map and draw an imaginary diagonal line from the Tees to the Exe. North and west of it is mostly upland and older, harder rock; south and east lowland and younger, softer rock. This is a simplification: Scotland's Central Lowlands and Northern Ireland's Lough Neagh basin are lowland in the north and west, and the Chilterns and South Downs are low hills in the south. Ask pupils to find exceptions.

teach.heading: Major upland areas
teach.note: Ask pupils to place each area on a blank outline map as you speak. Mention Mourne Mountains in Northern Ireland (Slieve Donard, 850 m). Heights are rounded and should be checked by the teacher, but they are standard figures. Ask: which is the highest point in the UK? (Ben Nevis.) Ask: which uplands are in England? Point out that these places link to the glacial landscapes studied later.

teach.heading: Major rivers
teach.note: The Severn is the UK's longest river (about 354 km) and the Thames the second longest (about 346 km); the Tay carries the largest volume of water (approx.). Ask pupils what pattern they notice (most flow east, to the North Sea, because rain falls on the western hills and the land slopes to the east and south). Ensure pupils can say 'flows from the ... to the ...'.

teach.heading: Skill: describe a pattern on a map

model.problem: Describe the distribution of upland areas in the UK. (3 marks)
steps: Overall pattern: the uplands are mainly in the north and west.
Named examples: the Scottish Highlands, Pennines, Lake District and Snowdonia.
Contrast: south and east are mainly lowland, such as East Anglia.
Use compass directions.
model.answer: Most upland areas are in the north and west of the UK. Examples include the Scottish Highlands, the Pennines and Snowdonia. The south and east, such as East Anglia, are mainly low-lying.

teach.note: I do. Describe, do not explain. Give compass directions and named places. Pupils lose marks with 'in the north' alone.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the longest river in the UK?
check.why: The Severn is the longest. Pupils often choose the Thames because it is more famous.

teach.note: Answer: B. Use as a prompt to say why fame is not length.

practice: Label an outline map of the UK with five upland areas and five rivers.
Write two sentences describing the pattern of rivers on your map.
independent: Core: Name three upland areas of the UK. (3 marks)
Extend: Describe the distribution of lowland areas in the UK. (3 marks)
Stretch: Suggest why most of the UK's high land is in the north and west. (4 marks)
exit: Name the longest river in the UK and where it flows.
Return to the big question: give one difference between the north-west and south-east.
lessons.homework: Create a one-page fact sheet on one UK upland area and one river, with a map.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-printed outline map with places to stick on. EAL: place names with pronunciation. Stretch: explain the link between rock type and relief.

lessons.unit: Unit 9: Coastal landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.2; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: Coastal processes: waves, weathering, erosion, transport and deposition
lessons.bigQuestion: How do waves shape the coastline?
objectives: Describe wave types and characteristics
Explain weathering and mass movement on coasts
Explain erosion, transport (including longshore drift) and deposition
successCriteria: All: name the two wave types and four erosion processes
Most: explain how longshore drift moves sediment
Some: explain how rock type and weather affect the speed of erosion
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: forces and energy transfer
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the power of the sea as a sign of creation

keywords.def: the distance of open water a wave has travelled over
water moving up the beach
water moving back down the beach
the zigzag movement of sediment along a coast by waves
the force of waves hitting cliffs, compressing air in cracks
waves hurling rocks at a cliff, wearing it away

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two upland areas of the UK.
What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
Define 'deposition'.

teach.heading: Wave types

left.title: Constructive waves
points: Low and long, spaced out
Strong swash, weak backwash
About 6 to 8 per minute
Build up the beach

right.title: Destructive waves
points: High and steep, close together
Weak swash, strong backwash
About 10 to 14 per minute
Erode the beach and cliff

teach.note: Wave size depends on the wind speed, wind duration and fetch. The UK's south-west faces the Atlantic with a long fetch, so it gets large waves. Constructive waves add material; destructive waves take it away. Ask pupils to recognise from a photo or a short clip. Misconception: constructive waves are always better; the beach can be built up in summer and eroded in winter storms.

teach.heading: Processes at the coast

head: Process
How it works
Example / note
rows: Freeze-thaw: water freezes in cracks, expands and breaks rock
Weak acid in rain dissolves rocks such as limestone and chalk
Rock slides, slumps or falls under gravity, often after rain
Soft clay cliffs slump; hard rock falls
Hydraulic power, abrasion, attrition and solution
Longshore drift moves material along the coast

teach.note: Link weathering to loosening of rock; erosion to wearing away by waves; mass movement to rock moving down a slope. Pupils usually confuse weathering and erosion: weathering breaks rock in place, erosion wears it away and carries it. Attrition is rocks hitting each other and becoming smaller and rounder; solution is dissolving of rock by seawater. Ask pupils which processes are likely to be quickest on a soft clay cliff (slumping and erosion).

teach.heading: Longshore drift
cycle: Waves approach at an angle because of the prevailing wind
Swash carries material up the beach at an angle
Backwash drags material straight down the slope
Material zigzags along the coast
Process repeats, moving sediment along the coast
teach.note: Draw a beach in plan view with arrows. Ask pupils to follow one pebble. In the UK, the prevailing wind is from the south-west so material generally moves from west to east along the south coast (check local direction before applying). Stress that drift builds beaches downdrift and deprives beaches updrift, which is why groynes are used. Link transport to deposition when waves lose energy.

teach.heading: Skill: explain a process

model.problem: Explain how longshore drift moves sediment along a coastline. (4 marks)
steps: Waves hit the coast at an angle because of the prevailing wind.
Swash carries sediment up the beach at that angle.
Backwash carries it straight back down due to gravity.
Repetition moves the sediment in a zigzag along the coast.
model.answer: Waves approach the coast at an angle because of the wind direction, so swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle. Backwash then pulls it straight back down because of gravity. This repeats many times, so sediment is moved along the coast in a zigzag.

teach.note: I do. Draw as you say. The four marks are four sequential steps. Pupils often forget the angle or say 'the waves go sideways'. Practise precise language.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which wave type has a strong backwash?
check.why: Destructive waves are steep, with weak swash and strong backwash that drags sediment away.

teach.note: Answer: B. Pupils choosing A often think that 'constructive' means strong; it is the opposite.

practice: Draw and label the two wave types; add one characteristic for each.
Complete a table of erosion processes with a one-line definition.
independent: Core: State two differences between constructive and destructive waves. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how hydraulic power erodes a cliff. (3 marks)
Stretch: Explain how weathering, mass movement and erosion work together to cause cliff retreat. (6 marks)
exit: Define longshore drift.
Return to the big question: give two processes that shape a coastline.
lessons.homework: Draw a diagram of longshore drift on a beach with five labels and a one-paragraph explanation.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-labelled process cards to sequence. EAL: use arrows and colours in diagrams. Stretch: explain why spits and groynes are linked to longshore drift.

lessons.unit: Unit 9: Coastal landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.2; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: Coastal landforms: headlands, caves, arches, stacks, beaches, spits and dunes
lessons.bigQuestion: How do the same waves make cliffs in one place and beaches in another?
objectives: Explain how geology and rock type shape coastal forms
Explain erosional landforms: headlands, bays, cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks
Explain depositional landforms: beaches, sand dunes, spits and bars
successCriteria: All: name the sequence from cave to stump and two depositional landforms
Most: explain how a headland and bay and a stack form, using a diagram
Some: explain how a spit forms and why rock type matters, with Dorset and Spurn Head as examples
lessons.crossCurricular: Geology and art: sketching and annotating landforms
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patterns and change in the earth shape our world

keywords.def: a piece of land jutting into the sea, made of resistant rock
a gently sloping rocky surface at the foot of a cliff
a column of rock separated from the headland
a long narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to land at one end
a ridge of sediment across a bay

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the processes of longshore drift in order.
State two differences between constructive and destructive waves.
Define 'abrasion'.

teach.heading: Geology matters

left.title: Resistant (hard) rock
points: Limestone, granite, chalk (in places)
Erodes slowly
Forms headlands, high cliffs, arches and stacks

right.title: Less resistant (soft) rock
points: Clay and sand
Erodes quickly
Forms bays and slumping cliffs

teach.note: Case study: the Dorset coast (Purbeck), a UK coastline with landforms. Bands of rock run at right angles to the sea. At Lulworth Cove, the sea broke through the resistant Portland limestone and eroded the softer clay and sands behind to form a circular cove. Durdle Door, a limestone arch, and Old Harry Rocks, chalk stacks near Swanage, are nearby. Draw a plan view with alternating hard and soft bands. Teachers should check local details against current guides.

teach.heading: From crack to stump

timeline.label: 1. Crack
timeline.text: Waves attack a weakness in the headland

timeline.label: 2. Cave
timeline.text: Hydraulic power and abrasion enlarge it

timeline.label: 3. Arch
timeline.text: The cave cuts through the headland, e.g. Durdle Door

timeline.label: 4. Stack
timeline.text: Weathering weakens the roof until it collapses, leaving a stack, e.g. Old Harry

timeline.label: 5. Stump
timeline.text: The stack is eroded to a small stump at the water

teach.note: Pupils should say 'waves attack' and name specific processes at each stage (hydraulic power, abrasion, weathering) to earn full marks. Wave-cut platform: waves undercut the base of a cliff, forming a notch; the cliff collapses and retreats, leaving a gently sloping platform that is exposed at low tide. Ask: why would a cliff of soft clay not produce a stack? (It would slump rather than stand as a column.)

teach.heading: Depositional landforms

head: Landform
How it forms
UK example
rows: Constructive waves deposit sand or shingle
Longshore drift deposits at a bend in the coast; the end curves with wind or waves
Spurn Head, Yorkshire; Hurst Castle Spit, Hampshire
A spit grows across a bay, trapping a lagoon
Wind blows dry sand inland; plants such as marram grass trap it

teach.note: Link to longshore drift from the previous lesson: spits grow in the direction of drift where the coastline turns. Sheltered water behind a spit allows salt marsh to develop. Dune formation: embryo dunes, foredunes, yellow dunes and grey dunes; plants such as marram grass stabilise them. Examples should be checked by the teacher; the principles matter most. Keep the focus on 'Explain how' wording.

teach.heading: Skill: explain landform formation

model.problem: Explain how a stack is formed. (4 marks)
steps: Start with a weakness: waves attack a crack in a headland.
Erosion enlarges it to a cave, then to an arch.
Weathering and erosion weaken the arch until the roof collapses.
The remaining column is a stack.
model.answer: Waves attack cracks in the headland and erode them into a cave through hydraulic power and abrasion. The cave is eroded through the headland to form an arch. Weathering and erosion weaken the arch until its roof collapses, which leaves a stack separated from the headland.

teach.note: I do. Draw labelled diagrams while talking. Require named processes. Pupils lose marks listing landforms without any process words.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which landform is formed by deposition?
check.why: A spit is built by longshore drift depositing sediment. The others are erosional.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Sketch and label a headland and bay; add the rock type for each.
Draw annotated diagrams of the stages from cave to stack.
independent: Core: Name two landforms formed by erosion and one by deposition. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how a spit is formed. (4 marks)
Stretch: Using a named UK coastline, explain how geology has influenced its landforms. (6 marks)
exit: Put cave, arch and stack in order.
Return to the big question: state one erosional and one depositional landform.
lessons.homework: Annotate a photograph or sketch of a coastal landform (such as Durdle Door or Spurn Head) with processes.
lessons.send: SEND: step cards for stages with diagrams. EAL: key words with labelled pictures. Stretch: explain the origins of Chesil Beach.

lessons.unit: Unit 9: Coastal landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.2; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: Managing the coast: hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat
lessons.bigQuestion: Should we fight the sea or work with it?
objectives: Describe hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat
Evaluate their costs and benefits
Use a UK scheme (Medmerry, West Sussex) to judge the success of managed realignment
successCriteria: All: name two hard and two soft strategies with one cost or benefit each
Most: explain how each strategy works and compare costs
Some: evaluate a real scheme and make a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: cost-benefit analysis; Citizenship: public decisions
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness: who is protected and who is not; guardianship of land and community

keywords.def: man-made structures built to stop erosion or flooding
working with natural processes to manage the coast
allowing the sea to flood or erode land in a controlled way
a wall built out from the beach to trap sediment
adding sand or shingle to a beach

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two depositional landforms.
State how longshore drift moves sediment.
What is a groyne used for? Say what you remember.

teach.heading: Coastal management strategies

head: Strategy
Type
How it works
Cost and issue
rows: Very expensive; can erode beach in front
Trap sediment from longshore drift to build beaches
Starves beaches further along the coast
Sand or shingle added to the beach
Sea is allowed to flood low-value land

teach.note: Sort by pupils: hard fights the sea; soft works with nature; managed retreat accepts change. Costs: hard structures cost millions (sea walls can cost about £5,000 to £10,000 per metre, approx.). Pupils should know there is no best option: it depends on what is being protected. Ask: if a farm field is at risk and a town is behind it, would you choose the same strategy for both? This prepares for the cost-benefit logic in the case study.

teach.heading: Case study: Medmerry managed realignment, West Sussex

head: Feature
Detail
rows: A narrow shingle bank was repeatedly breached; flooding risk to homes, a holiday park, roads and a water treatment works
New inland embankments about 7 km long built; the old shingle bank was breached in 2013, allowing tidal flooding of farmland
Protects over 300 properties (approx.); creates about 180 hectares of new habitat for birds and wildlife (approx.); tourism
Farmland lost; compulsory purchase; some objections

teach.note: This is a recent managed realignment, among the largest in Europe at the time. Check the figures before use: they are approximate. Explain why this is cheaper in the long term: the sea takes the pressure and a natural saltmarsh and mudflat absorbs wave energy. Ask: who benefits and who loses? (Residents and wildlife gain; the farmer loses land.) For a hard engineering comparison you may add Mappleton, Holderness (1991, rock groynes and rock armour) but this is optional.

teach.heading: Skill: evaluate a scheme

model.problem: Assess the success of a coastal management scheme you have studied. (6 marks, outline)
steps: Aim: what was the scheme meant to do? (protect homes and create habitat at Medmerry)
Benefits with detail: over 300 properties protected; new wildlife habitat.
Costs with detail: about £28 million; farmland lost.
Judgement: successful overall because the cost is justified and the solution is sustainable, though some people lost land.
model.answer: Medmerry was designed to protect homes on the Selsey peninsula and create wildlife habitat. It protects over 300 properties and has created large areas of salt marsh, but it cost about £28 million and farmers lost land. Overall it is successful because it provides lasting protection at a reasonable cost, although some people lost out.

teach.note: I do. Show the balanced structure and ask pupils to circle the figure and the judgement. Insist on a clear answer to 'how successful'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is an example of soft engineering?
check.why: Beach nourishment adds natural sediment. The others are hard engineering.

teach.note: Answer: C. Some pupils think groynes are soft because they are small; they are still a built structure.

practice: Complete a table of strategies with one advantage and one disadvantage each.
Rank the strategies for a village with 50 homes and give reasons.
independent: Core: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a sea wall. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain why managed retreat may be chosen instead of hard engineering. (4 marks)
Stretch: Using a named UK scheme, evaluate the success of coastal management. (6 marks)
exit: Name one hard and one soft engineering strategy.
Return to the big question: give a view in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word letter to a councillor arguing for either hard engineering or managed retreat for a village at risk.
lessons.send: SEND: sort cards for hard / soft / retreat. EAL: sentence frames for advantage/disadvantage. Stretch: consider who decides what to protect and how costs are shared.

lessons.unit: Unit 10: River landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.3; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: River processes and the changing profile from source to mouth
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a river look so different near its source and its mouth?
objectives: Describe the long profile and changing cross profile of a river and valley
Explain erosion, transportation and deposition in rivers
Describe how channel features change downstream
successCriteria: All: describe the upper, middle and lower course
Most: explain river erosion and transport processes
Some: explain why the load, velocity and channel change downstream
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading graphs of gradient and discharge; Science: forces
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: water as a precious, life-giving resource and our duty not to waste it

keywords.def: a side view of a river from source to mouth
a slice across a river channel and valley
the force of water on the banks and bed
the river's load scraping and wearing the bed and banks
large stones rolled along the river bed

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three UK rivers and where they flow to.
What is erosion?
Describe the difference between weathering and erosion.

teach.heading: Changes downstream
teach.note: Draw a long profile as a smooth concave curve from steep to flat. Link channel size to discharge, which increases as tributaries join. Velocity usually increases downstream even though the gradient decreases, because the larger channel has less friction; pupils find this surprising. The Bradshaw model describes these changes: width, depth, discharge, velocity and load size. Ask: why is the load rounder downstream? (Attrition.)

teach.heading: Erosion and transport

left.title: Erosion
points: Hydraulic action: force of water in cracks
Abrasion: load scrapes the bed and banks
Attrition: stones collide and become smaller and rounder
Solution: soluble rock dissolves

right.title: Transport
points: Traction: large stones rolled along the bed
Saltation: smaller stones bounced along the bed
Suspension: fine silt carried in the water
Solution: dissolved material carried

teach.note: Pupils can match each process to the size of the load. In flood the river's energy is higher so it can move larger material. Deposition occurs when the river loses energy, for example when it floods, slows around a bend or enters the sea. Misconception: rivers only erode at the source. Erosion and deposition occur all the way along.

teach.heading: Skill: explain a downstream change

model.problem: Explain why the size of the river's load decreases downstream. (3 marks)
steps: Stones collide with each other and the bed: attrition.
This breaks them into smaller, rounder pieces.
Larger material is deposited when the river loses energy.
model.answer: Stones in the river are worn down by attrition as they collide with each other and the bed, so they get smaller and rounder as they move downstream. Heavy material is also deposited when the river's energy drops.

teach.note: I do. Each mark is a process-and-result pair. Pupils often say 'because it gets eroded' without naming attrition.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which process is the main cause of valley deepening in the upper course?
check.why: In the upper course the river cuts down, forming a V-shaped valley. Lateral erosion is more important in the middle course.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Draw a long profile and add labels for upper, middle and lower course with two features each.
Match each transport process to the load it carries.
independent: Core: Describe how the valley shape changes from the upper to the lower course. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how a river erodes its channel. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain why a river's velocity and load change downstream. (6 marks)
exit: Name two erosion processes.
Return to the big question: give two differences between the upper and lower course.
lessons.homework: Draw a fully annotated long profile with processes and landforms for each course.
lessons.send: SEND: annotated long profile template with word bank. EAL: key words with diagrams. Stretch: explain why velocity increases downstream despite gentler gradient.

lessons.unit: Unit 10: River landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.3; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: River landforms: waterfalls to estuaries on the River Tees
lessons.bigQuestion: How does one river carve and build so many different landforms?
objectives: Explain landforms: interlocking spurs, waterfalls, gorges, meanders, ox-bow lakes, levees, flood plains and estuaries
Describe how these landforms appear along a UK river valley, the River Tees
Use diagrams to explain formation
successCriteria: All: name the landform for each course of the river
Most: explain how a waterfall and gorge or a meander forms
Some: explain the full sequence of ox-bow lake formation and link it to the Tees
lessons.crossCurricular: Art and skills: annotated diagrams; OS map skills
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the endless work of flowing water as a sign of creation

keywords.def: ridges of land that stick out alternately on either side of the river in the upper course
a sudden drop of the river over a step in the river bed
a narrow, steep-sided valley left as a waterfall retreats
a bend in the river
a curved lake left when a meander is cut off
a natural raised bank formed by deposits during floods

starter: Say Bismillah. Describe the upper course of a river.
What are the processes of transport in a river?
State two differences between upper and lower course.

teach.heading: Case study: the River Tees (north-east England)

head: Course
Landform
Where on the Tees
rows: Upper (Pennines, Cross Fell source, about 893 m)
High Force (about 21 m) and Low Force, over the hard Whin Sill
Between Barnard Castle and Yarm: Yarm sits within a meander
Tees estuary at Middlesbrough and Teesmouth, North Sea

teach.note: The Tees is about 137 km long (approx.). Use an OS map extract if available: high contour density in the upper course and wide flat valley near Yarm. Check heights and distances before use. High Force's drop of about 21 m is widely quoted. Ask pupils to say how the landforms change from the Pennines to the sea and link back to the profile lesson.

teach.heading: Waterfall and gorge formation
cycle: Hard rock overlies soft rock
Water erodes the soft rock beneath faster, creating an overhang
Overhang collapses; plunge pool deepens by hydraulic action and abrasion
The waterfall retreats upstream
A steep-sided gorge is left
teach.note: At High Force the hard dolerite (Whin Sill) caps softer sedimentary rock. Draw the cross-section and use arrows. Ask: where is the plunge pool? Pupils must use process words and the term 'retreats'. The gorge is the evidence of past retreat.

teach.heading: Meander to ox-bow lake
cycle: Faster flow on the outside bend erodes a river cliff
Slower flow on the inside deposits a slip-off slope
Bends become more curved; the neck narrows
In flood the river breaks through the neck
Deposition seals off the old bend: an ox-bow lake
teach.note: Draw a plan view and cross-section. Pupils often say 'water goes faster on the inside'. It is faster on the outside. Meanders migrate sideways and downstream across the flood plain. Ox-bow lakes eventually dry into marshy ground (a meander scar).

teach.heading: Flood plains, levees and estuaries
bullets: In floods, the river spills over and deposits silt on the flood plain.
Coarser material drops first near the banks, building levees.
Fine silt makes the flood plain flat and fertile.
At the estuary, tides and deposition form mud flats and salt marsh.
teach.note: Explain why people farm and build on flood plains (fertile, flat, near water) even though they flood. Levees can be heightened by people; link to flood management later. Estuaries are tidal and have deposited mud; the Tees Estuary is also heavily industrial. Ask: why do rivers deposit at the mouth? (Velocity drops and the water meets the sea.)

teach.heading: Skill: explain landform formation

model.problem: Explain how an ox-bow lake is formed. (4 marks)
steps: Erosion on the outside bend and deposition on the inside make the meander more curved.
The neck of the meander gets narrower.
In a flood the river cuts through the neck, taking a new, shorter route.
Deposition seals the ends of the old bend, leaving a lake.
model.answer: Erosion on the outside bends and deposition on the inside make a meander more curved and the neck narrow. In a flood the river cuts through the neck and takes the shortest route. Deposition then seals off the old meander, leaving an ox-bow lake.

teach.note: I do. Draw each stage. Stress the link between flood and breakthrough. Pupils often forget deposition is what seals the lake.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: On a meander, where does erosion mainly occur?
options: Only in the middle of the channel
check.why: Flow is fastest on the outside bend, so it erodes a river cliff. Deposition is on the inside bend.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Draw annotated diagrams for the formation of a waterfall and an ox-bow lake.
Annotate a map or photo of the Tees valley with at least four landforms.
independent: Core: Name three landforms of the upper course. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how a waterfall and gorge are formed. (4 marks)
Stretch: Using a named UK river valley, explain how its landforms change from source to mouth. (6 marks)
exit: Name one landform of erosion and one of deposition.
Return to the big question: link one landform to erosion and one to deposition.
lessons.homework: Create a fact sheet for the River Tees with a sketch map and four annotated landforms.
lessons.send: SEND: step cards for formation diagrams. EAL: pictures and arrows. Stretch: explain why High Force is retreating at a slow rate.

lessons.unit: Unit 10: River landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.3; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: Flooding: causes, hydrographs and the Jubilee River scheme
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it better to control a river or to live with its floods?
objectives: Explain flood risk factors: precipitation, geology, relief and land use
Interpret hydrographs showing the precipitation-discharge relationship
Evaluate hard and soft engineering with a UK flood management scheme
successCriteria: All: name four factors that increase flood risk
Most: read a hydrograph for lag time and peak discharge
Some: evaluate a scheme and make a judgement using costs and benefits
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading and interpreting graphs; Citizenship: public decision-making
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness: when protecting one town increases risk to another

keywords.def: the volume of water flowing past a point in a given time, in cumecs (cubic metres per second)
the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge
a graph showing river discharge and rainfall over time
does not allow water to pass through
a man-made channel that carries flood water away from a town

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three landforms found on a flood plain.
Define 'deposition'.
Why do people live on flood plains?

teach.heading: Flood risk factors

head: Factor
Effect on flooding
rows: Long, heavy rain or rapid snow melt; already wet ground raises risk
Impermeable rock such as clay or granite causes fast runoff; porous rock soaks water in
Steep slopes send water quickly to rivers; flat land floods slowly
Urban surfaces and drains send water fast; trees intercept and slow it

teach.note: Ask pupils to design the 'worst case' catchment: steep, impermeable, urban, with prolonged rain. Link factors to speed of runoff (surface water reaching the river). Human effects: urbanisation and deforestation raise risk; climate change may increase rainfall intensity. Flood risk in the UK also depends on tides at the coast and on groundwater.

teach.heading: Reading a hydrograph (data to plot)
teach.note: Pupils plot discharge as a line and rainfall as bars. Key terms: peak discharge (60 cumecs at 15:00), lag time (peak rainfall at 09:00 and peak discharge at 15:00, so lag is 6 hours), rising limb, falling limb and baseflow (about 5 cumecs). A flashy hydrograph has a short lag time and high peak: steep, impermeable, urban. A gentle one has a long lag time and low peak. Ask: how would the graph change if the catchment were urbanised? (Shorter lag time, higher peak.)

teach.heading: Managing floods

left.title: Hard engineering
points: Dams and reservoirs store flood water
Straightening the channel speeds water away
Embankments raise banks
Relief channels divert flood water

right.title: Soft engineering
points: Flood warnings and preparation
Flood-zone planning: no building on the flood plain
Tree planting slows runoff
River restoration and wetlands

teach.note: Hard engineering protects places strongly but is expensive and can increase risk downstream. Soft engineering is cheaper and more natural but offers less certain protection. Ask: which would a town with 5,000 homes choose? Link to cost-benefit decisions. Mention that straightening a channel moves flood water faster to places downstream, which is why it is often avoided today.

teach.heading: Case study: the Jubilee River, Thames valley

head: Feature
Detail
rows: A relief channel about 11.6 km long, from Maidenhead to Windsor and Eton (Berkshire)
Large floods, such as 1947, threatened Maidenhead, Windsor and Eton
Built by the Environment Agency in the 1990s to 2002; diverts water around the towns in flood
Protects thousands of properties (approx. 5,000); creates a wildlife corridor and a footpath
Very expensive; flood risk may rise for some communities downstream; some leaks and repairs

teach.note: Choose this case study, or substitute another UK scheme such as Banbury or Boscastle if the class prefers; the figures here are approximate and should be checked by the teacher against Environment Agency sources before the lesson. Ask: who benefits and who might lose? Link to the Thames, which was studied earlier. Use the lesson on managing floods to rehearse the 'assess' style of question.

teach.heading: Skill: interpret a hydrograph

model.problem: Using the hydrograph data, describe the lag time and the peak discharge. (3 marks)
steps: Peak discharge: the highest value was 60 cumecs at 15:00.
Lag time: rainfall peaked at 09:00, so lag time was 6 hours.
Add a comparison with baseflow: discharge rose from 5 to 60 cumecs.
model.answer: The peak discharge was 60 cumecs at 15:00. Rainfall peaked at 09:00 so the lag time was 6 hours. Discharge rose from 5 cumecs to 60 cumecs, showing a big increase.

teach.note: I do. Insist on units and times. Many pupils confuse lag time with the length of the storm; it runs from peak rainfall to peak discharge.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which change would shorten the lag time of a river?
options: Building houses and roads across the catchment
check.why: Impermeable urban surfaces and drains speed runoff, shortening lag time and raising the peak.

teach.note: Answer: B. Pupils choosing A have reversed the effect; trees intercept rain and lengthen lag time.

practice: Plot the hydrograph from the table and label peak discharge, lag time, rising limb and falling limb.
Sort flood strategies into hard and soft and give one advantage and one disadvantage for each.
independent: Core: Give two physical factors that increase flood risk. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how urbanisation changes a hydrograph. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the success of a UK flood management scheme. (6 marks)
exit: Define lag time.
Return to the big question: give a reason to control floods and a reason to live with them.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word briefing for a council on whether to build a new flood wall or restore wetlands upstream.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn hydrograph axes and key-term word bank. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: compare hard engineering schemes with natural flood management.

lessons.unit: Unit 11: Glacial landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.4; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: Ice ages and glacial processes in the UK
lessons.bigQuestion: How did ice sculpt the UK's mountains and valleys?
objectives: Describe the maximum extent of UK ice cover in the last ice age
Explain freeze-thaw weathering, plucking and abrasion
Explain glacial movement and deposition
successCriteria: All: name three processes of glacial erosion and say where the ice reached
Most: explain freeze-thaw and plucking in order
Some: explain why glacial processes produce different landforms in different places
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: states of matter and expansion on freezing
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: change over vast time; humility before the history of the Earth

keywords.def: a large mass of ice that moves slowly downhill
weathering when water freezes in cracks, expands and breaks rock
ice freezes to rock and pulls pieces away as it moves
rocks frozen in the ice scrape and scratch the valley
unsorted rock debris dropped by melting ice

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two UK upland areas.
Define 'weathering'.
Why does frozen water break rock?

teach.heading: The last ice age in the UK
bullets: The Devensian ice sheet peaked about 20,000 years ago (approx.).
Ice covered Scotland, Wales, northern England and parts of the Midlands.
Southern England was bitterly cold tundra.
Ice melted about 10,000 to 15,000 years ago.
teach.note: Show a map with the maximum extent of ice: it covered all of Scotland and most of Wales, with the south limit around the Bristol Channel in the west and North Norfolk coast in the east. Ice was up to a kilometre or more thick in places (approx.). Ask pupils why upland areas also grew their own glaciers (cold, snow). Pupils need only describe the extent: use 'north of a line from...'. Dates are approximate; check the latest consensus.

teach.heading: Freeze-thaw weathering
cycle: Water enters cracks in the rock
At night it freezes and expands by about 9%
Pressure widens the crack
It thaws by day and water goes deeper
Repeated cycles break off pieces, forming scree
teach.note: Demonstrate expansion with a sealed bottle of water in a freezer if possible (take care). The process needs temperatures that swing about freezing, as on upland slopes in winter. Scree collects beneath cliffs. Misconception: freeze-thaw only happens in glaciers; it is common in the UK uplands today.

teach.heading: Erosion processes

left.title: Plucking
points: Meltwater freezes onto rock
Ice moves and pulls out chunks
Leaves jagged, steep faces
Typical of back walls and valley steps

right.title: Abrasion
points: Rocks frozen in the ice scrape the surface
Like sandpaper, it smooths and scratches
Deepens and widens valleys
Leaves scratches called striations

teach.note: Draw a glacier in cross-section showing debris at its base. Add rotational movement in corries and basal sliding of ice on meltwater. Ice bulldozes loose material. Deposition occurs when ice melts and the load is dropped as unsorted till. Ask pupils: why does plucking leave a jagged surface while abrasion makes it smooth?

teach.heading: Skill: explain a process

model.problem: Explain how plucking and abrasion erode a glacial valley. (4 marks)
steps: Plucking: meltwater freezes to the valley sides and bed.
As the glacier moves it pulls pieces of rock away.
Abrasion: rocks embedded in the ice scrape the surface like sandpaper.
Result: the valley is widened, deepened and smoothed.
model.answer: In plucking, meltwater freezes onto the rock and as the glacier moves it pulls pieces away. In abrasion, rocks frozen into the base of the glacier scrape the rock like sandpaper. Together they widen and deepen the valley.

teach.note: I do. Pupils muddle the two processes. Plucking pulls; abrasion scrapes. Give a gesture for each.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which process involves ice pulling rock away as it moves?
check.why: Plucking: the ice freezes to the rock and pulls it away.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Shade the extent of the Devensian ice on an outline map of the UK and label three areas.
Sequence the stages of freeze-thaw and draw a diagram.
independent: Core: Describe the maximum extent of ice in the last ice age in the UK. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how freeze-thaw weathering breaks rock. (3 marks)
Stretch: Explain how glacial erosion processes work together to deepen a valley. (6 marks)
exit: Define 'plucking'.
Return to the big question: name two processes ice uses to shape land.
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled glacier diagram with freeze-thaw, plucking, abrasion and deposition marked.
lessons.send: SEND: process cards with pictures. EAL: use gestures and diagrams. Stretch: explain why ice flow differs in a corrie and in a valley glacier.

lessons.unit: Unit 11: Glacial landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.4; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: Glacial landforms of erosion and deposition: the Lake District
lessons.bigQuestion: What evidence of ice can we still see in today's landscape?
objectives: Explain erosional landforms: corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, troughs, ribbon lakes and hanging valleys
Explain transport and deposition landforms: erratics, drumlins and moraines
Use the Lake District as a case study of a glaciated upland
successCriteria: All: name and sketch four glacial landforms
Most: explain how a corrie and an arête form
Some: explain the formation of glacial troughs, ribbon lakes and drumlins using a named upland
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: sketching landforms; Skills: OS map interpretation
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at landscapes shaped by immense forces over time

keywords.def: a bowl-shaped hollow high on a mountain, cut by ice
a sharp ridge between two corries
a spur cut off by a glacier
a long narrow lake in a glacial trough
an egg-shaped hill of till
a ridge of rock debris deposited by a glacier

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three processes of glacial erosion.
Describe the extent of the ice sheet in the UK.
Define 'freeze-thaw'.

teach.heading: Formation of a corrie

timeline.label: 1. Snow collects
timeline.text: Snow gathers in a hollow on a north- or east-facing slope; it turns to ice

timeline.label: 2. Freeze-thaw
timeline.text: Weathering loosens the back wall and nivation enlarges the hollow

timeline.label: 3. Rotation
timeline.text: The ice rotates, deepening the floor by abrasion; plucking steepens the back wall

timeline.label: 4. Retreat
timeline.text: When the ice melts, a steep back wall, a bowl and a rock lip remain

timeline.label: 5. Tarn
timeline.text: Water fills the hollow, forming a tarn such as Red Tarn on Helvellyn

teach.note: Corrie: also called cirque or cwm. Pupils should include freeze-thaw, plucking, abrasion and rotational slip. Stress that the hollow faces the direction that is shadier (in the UK the north-east). Ask: where is the rock lip, and why does it form? (Less erosion at the front where ice thins.) Link to Helvellyn in the Lake District: Red Tarn sits in a corrie and Striding Edge is an arête.

teach.heading: Erosional landforms

head: Landform
How it forms
Lake District / UK example
rows: Two corries erode back to back, leaving a knife-edge ridge
Three or more corries erode a mountain
A glacier deepens and straightens a river valley into a U-shape
Glacier cuts off the ends of spurs
Water fills an over-deepened part of the trough
A tributary valley left high above the trough; a waterfall forms

teach.note: Draw a cross-section of a glacial trough: U-shape, truncated spurs, hanging valleys on the sides, ribbon lake on the floor. Windermere is about 17 km long (approx.); Wastwater, England's deepest lake at about 79 m (approx.). Check examples against a good source before use; the principles are what AQA tests. Ask: why do trough sides appear steep? (Abrasion and plucking at the base and sides.)

teach.heading: Transport and deposition landforms

head: Landform
Description
Example
rows: Rocks carried a long way and dropped on different rock types
Egg-shaped hills of till; steeper end faces the ice, gently tapered end shows direction
Ridges of debris: lateral (sides), medial (centre), terminal (furthest advance)

teach.note: Ice transports material by bulldozing (pushing), by carrying debris on top, within and under the glacier. When the ice melts, the debris is dropped as till. Pupils must know the difference between a lateral and a terminal moraine. Norber erratics are boulders of Silurian rock sitting on limestone. The drumlin example is approximate: check with a local atlas or OS map.

teach.heading: Skill: explain formation of a landform

model.problem: Explain how an arête is formed. (3 marks)
steps: Two corries form on opposite sides of a mountain.
Plucking and abrasion erode their back walls so they cut backwards.
The land between them becomes a narrow, steep-sided ridge: the arête.
model.answer: Two corries form back to back on opposite sides of a mountain. Plucking and abrasion make the back walls retreat, which leaves a narrow, knife-edge ridge between them, called an arête.

teach.note: I do. Sketch it in two stages. The key is the idea of back-to-back erosion: pupils just say 'it is a ridge'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which landform is made by deposition?
check.why: Drumlins are hills of till deposited by ice. The others are erosional.

teach.note: Answer: C.

lessons.title: The Lake District: land use, conflict and managing tourism
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a beautiful landscape be shared between visitors, farmers and wildlife?
objectives: Describe economic activities in glaciated uplands: tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying
Discuss land-use conflicts and tensions between development and conservation
Explain impacts and management of tourism in the Lake District
successCriteria: All: name four land uses and one conflict
Most: explain impacts of tourism and how they are managed
Some: evaluate how effective management has been and reach a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: opportunity cost; Citizenship: planning and local democracy
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship of land; fairness between visitors and local people

keywords.def: a place that attracts large numbers of visitors
a protected area with strict planning rules
disagreement between groups wanting different uses of the same land
wearing away of paths by walkers
tourism that can continue without harming the environment

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two glacial landforms of the Lake District.
Define 'ribbon lake'.
State one possible use of an upland area.

teach.heading: Economic activities in glaciated uplands

head: Activity
Why here
Problem
rows: Rough pasture; sheep such as Herdwicks
Thin soils, steep slopes and harsh weather; low incomes
Conifers grow on poor soils at altitude
Plantations change the landscape and wildlife
Hard rocks such as slate and granite
Noise, dust, lorries and scars on the landscape

teach.note: Ask pupils which activities are traditional and which are modern. In the Lake District, Honister is a working slate mine and Grizedale and Whinlatter are forests. Hill farming is part of the cultural landscape, and was recognised when the Lake District became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017 (check wording). Keep the principle clear: glaciated uplands have steep slopes, thin soils and scenery.

teach.heading: A land-use conflict

left.title: Development and visitors
points: Tourism supports jobs and income
Second homes and shops serve visitors
Quarries and forestry supply materials
Roads and car parks needed

right.title: Conservation and residents
points: Traffic jams and noise upset residents
Second homes push up house prices
Footpath erosion and habitat damage
Farming and wildlife need space

teach.note: Ask pupils to role-play a public meeting: a hotel owner, a farmer, a walker, a conservation officer. Highlight that the Lake District has about 40,000 residents but welcomes many millions of visits each year (about 18 million, approx.; check the latest figures). Conflicts include second homes, jam-packed roads in summer and speedboats on Windermere (a 10 mph limit was introduced in 2005, approx.).

teach.heading: Case study: tourism in the Lake District National Park

head: Impact
Management
rows: Footpath erosion on popular fells such as Helvellyn
Path repairs by volunteers and groups (for example Fix the Fells); stone pitching and re-routing
Traffic and car parking at honeypots such as Ambleside and Keswick
Park-and-ride, buses and cycle routes; parking charges
Speed limit of 10 mph on Windermere
Planning rules and local housing policies
Education, wardens and sustainable tourism messages

teach.note: The Lake District became a national park in 1951 and covers about 2,362 square kilometres (approx.). The park authority balances conservation and recreation. Ask: which strategy do you think works best and why? Possible answers include education, since it changes behaviour, or path repairs, since they fix the damage directly. Check present policies; they change. Remind pupils that exam answers should name the place and a specific scheme.

teach.heading: Skill: assess management

model.problem: Assess the effectiveness of management of tourism in a named glaciated upland. (6 marks, outline)
steps: Problem with detail: footpath erosion on Helvellyn from large numbers of walkers.
Management: path repair projects with stone steps and re-routing.
Strength: it reduces erosion and keeps the paths usable.
Weakness: costly and relies on volunteers; visitor numbers keep rising.
Judgement: effective locally, but needs to be combined with limits on traffic and visitor education.
model.answer: In the Lake District, thousands of walkers cause footpath erosion on fells such as Helvellyn. Path repairs with stone steps reduce erosion and keep paths safe, but they are costly and depend on volunteers while visitor numbers keep growing. Overall the repairs are effective locally but work best alongside traffic management and education.

teach.note: I do. Show pupils to use named places and a clear judgement. Many answers stay general: 'visitors cause damage and rangers fix it'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: What is a honeypot site?
options: A site with a lot of wildlife
A place which attracts many visitors
check.why: A honeypot is a place that draws large numbers of visitors, such as Ambleside or Bowness-on-Windermere.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Complete a table of land uses with one opportunity and one conflict each for the Lake District.
Role-play: write a 30-second statement for a farmer, a walker and a resident.
independent: Core: Give two economic activities found in glaciated uplands. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain one conflict between land uses in a glaciated upland. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess the effectiveness of managing tourism in a named UK glaciated upland. (6 marks)
exit: Name one impact of tourism and one management strategy.
Return to the big question: give a reason for sharing and one challenge.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word letter to the National Park Authority suggesting one way to reduce the impact of tourism.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-structured table for impacts and management. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: compare management in the Lake District with another national park.
